paper.title: MedReason: Eliciting Factual Medical Reasoning Steps in LLMs via Knowledge Graphs

author.affiliation: Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard University and Chungnam National University

paper.abstract: Medical tasks such as diagnosis and treatment planning require precise and complex reasoning, particularly in life-critical domains. Unlike mathematical reasoning, medical reasoning demands meticulous, verifiable thought processes to ensure reliability and accuracy. However, there is a notable lack of datasets that provide transparent, step-by-step reasoning to validate and enhance the medical reasoning ability of AI models. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MedReason**, a large-scale high-quality medical reasoning dataset designed to enable faithful and explainable medical problem-solving in large language models (LLMs). We utilize a structured medical knowledge graph (KG) to convert clinical QA pairs into logical chains of reasoning, or “thinking paths”, which trace connections from question elements to answers via relevant KG entities. Each path is validated for consistency with clinical logic and evidence-based medicine. Our pipeline generates detailed reasoning for various medical questions from 7 medical datasets, resulting in a dataset of **32,682** question-answer pairs, each with detailed, step-by-step explanations. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning with our dataset consistently boosts medical problem-solving capabilities, achieving significant gains of up to **7.7%** for DeepSeek-Ditill-8B. Our top-performing model, MedReason-8B, outperforms the Huatuo-o1-8B, a state-of-the-art medical reasoning model, by up to **4.2%** on the clinical benchmark MedBullets. We also engage medical professionals from diverse specialties to assess our dataset’s quality, ensuring MedReason offers accurate and coherent medical reasoning. Our data, models, and code will be publicly available.

paper.title: AAgiSphere-CORE: A Multi-Dimensional Co-Optimization Framework for Autonomous Prescriptive Maintenance in Smart Manufacturing
paper.abstract: Intelligent workflows for smart manufacturing reliability and maintenance (RxM) are transitioning from static, sequential multi-agent systems toward autonomous, dynamic decision-making. However, a critical gap persists between agent coordination and the holistic co-optimization required across predictive performance, computational resources, and domain-specific business logic. To address this, we propose AgiSphere-CORE, a novel framework centered on a Co-Optimization Core (COC). The COC maintains a unified Collaborative State Vector and solves a constrained optimization problem to maximize the Collaborative Utility J_{co}, dynamically orchestrating specialized agents for resources, models, and logic. This enables a paradigm shift from sequential to co-optimization-driven autonomy. Extensive evaluation on multiple manufacturing tasks, including classification, regression, and anomaly detection, demonstrates that AgiSphere-CORE consistently outperforms baselines, achieving superior predictive performance (e.g., 97.3% accuracy, 0.902 F1-score), improved resource efficiency (15% faster workflow time), and higher estimated domain cost savings ($148.7K). Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the COC and the adaptive learning mechanism. A detailed case study further illustrates the framework’s transparent, utility-driven trade-offs. We conclude that AgiSphere-CORE provides a robust, holistic foundation for next-generation autonomous RxM systems in smart manufacturing.

paper.title: MSRA: A Parameter-Efficient Spectral Correction for Local Attention — Where It Helps, and Where It Fails
paper.abstract: Restricting attention to a sliding window makes long documents affordable, but it discards everything beyond the window. This paper asks what can be recovered when the model is already trained, its weights are frozen, and the budget for new parameters is only a few tens of thousands. We propose Multi-scale Spectral Residual Attention (MSRA): a far-field branch grafted onto the last few layers of a frozen model, which condenses out-of-window history through smoothly distance-decayed weights and adds it back to the attention output—roughly 9K–45K trainable parameters, plus minimal 8-to-16-scalar probes for attribution. On PG-19 long-form fiction, the branch closes up to 31.7% of the perplexity gap between local and full attention, with gains stable across two architectures, multiple seeds, and the official test partition. The attribution proves sharper than the headline: 16 learnable output-gain scalars alone close 26.4%, returns accelerate with grafting depth, the carefully designed kernel structure and gating contribute only secondarily—and a budget-matched LoRA closes 87.4%, indicating that the gap is mostly generic capacity rather than a missing far-field pathway. Retrieval experiments complete the map: the correction is a statistical smoother that helps just beyond the window, slightly hurts precise in-window prediction, recovers essentially nothing at genuine long distance, and does not transfer to task metrics—while slowing prefill two-to-three-fold and leaving decoding unaffected. These results bound what a lightweight spectral correction can and cannot recover, forming a reproducible decision reference for local long-context design.

paper.title: Trust-Aware Multi-Axis Reliability Auditing for NLP Classifiers: A Theoretical and Empirical Framework
paper.abstract: Accuracy remains the dominant criterion for selecting NLP classifiers, yet it fails to characterize the operational reliability required for deployment under class imbalance, distribution shift, and demographic heterogeneity. We introduce TNMM++ (Trustworthy NLP Multi-axis Monitoring, extended), a theoretically grounded reliability audit that evaluates classifiers along seven complementary axes, utility, calibration, robustness, safety, fairness, selective prediction, and uncertainty quantification, and formalises model selection as constrained multi-objective optimization. Beyond metric aggregation, TNMM++ contributes six algorithmic results: a reliability tensor, a Pareto convex-hull theorem, variance-adaptive weighting, a boundary-predictor criterion with exclusion rule for majority-class collapse, a Bayesian risk decomposition, and the TAMS algorithm with optimality bound. Evaluating eight lightweight Transformer encoders (MiniLM, ELECTRA, mBERT, DistilBERT, MobileBERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, XLM-R) and excluding models that failed to learn the task, we find that properly trained mid-tier models exhibit balanced utility and calibration superior to collapsed high-accuracy counterparts. TrustScore identifies mBERT (0.6685), ELECTRA (0.6630), and DistilBERT (0.6627) as deployment-reliable. Sensitivity analysis under 1,000 Dirichlet weight perturbations confirms ranking stability in 92.4% of configurations, and multi-seed evaluation (5 seeds) demonstrates conclusions are not seed artifacts. Our findings establish that single-metric selection is statistically unreliable and motivate multi-axis reliability auditing as the default protocol for trustworthy NLP deployment.

paper.title: VERITYGATE: A Four-Gate Schema-Level Faithfulness Framework and Paired Benchmark for Grounded LLM Narrations over Structured Evidence

author.affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder and ebay Inc.

paper.abstract: Fluent LLM explanations may not follow the evidence from a structured system. We present VERITYGATE, a four-gate checker for declared evidence IDs, entities, numbers, and claim types. It checks a fixed schema; it does not verify every fact in the prose. At r=0 and r=1, we test 900 instances per setting (450 grounded–ungrounded pairs) with GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Under this schema-level contract and before repair, 80.3% of mini claims and 47.9% of Sonnet claims fail. These are verifier rejection rates, not prose-hallucination rates. One repair pass raises claim survival from 19.7% to 28.0% for mini and from 52.1% to 54.3% for Sonnet. Verified claims per example change by +0.14 for mini, −0.71 for Llama, and −0.47 for Sonnet, so survival and output volume must be reported together. A second Sonnet pass gives no clear gain. At r=1, Gate 4 covers 97.0%, 98.7%, and 100% of failing claims for mini, Llama, and Sonnet. Small human studies support the rules but show gaps between schema checks and correct prose. A domain-specific GPT-4o judge test shows an order effect, so it is only a usefulness check. We release the code and data.

paper.title: EVO-RAG: Evolving Retrieval-Augmented Agents for Efficient Multi-Hop Query Optimization
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds large language models (LLMs) in external evidence, yet multi-hop pipelines still suffer from redundant sub-queries, shallow exploration, and premature or delayed stopping. We present EVO-RAG, a phase-aware framework that couples a lightweight two-stage curriculum (Discovery→Refinement) with seven step-level rewards and an in-episode time scheduler. The scheduler decays exploration incentives as evidence accumulates while increasing efficiency and correctness pressure as uncertainty shrinks. Beyond scalar rewards, we train a multi-head preference model and benchmark DPO, PPO, and GRPO under identical rollouts and curricula for a controlled comparison. Evaluated on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle with 8B-class backbones, EVO-RAG improves EM/F1 while reducing redundant hops. Ablations show that suppressing query overlap, rewarding controlled backtracking and justified refusal, and time-dynamic weighting are key to the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

paper.title: Retrieval–Reasoning Processes for Multi-hop Question Answering: A Four-Axis Design Framework and Empirical Trends
paper.abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires systems to iteratively retrieve evidence and reason across multiple hops. While recent RAG and agentic methods report strong results, the underlying retrieval–reasoning process is often left implicit, making procedural choices hard to compare across model families. This survey takes the execution procedure as the unit of analysis and introduces a four-axis framework covering overall execution plan, index structure, next-step control strategies and triggers, and stop/continue criteria. Using this schema, we map representative multi-hop QA systems and synthesize reported ablations and empirical tendencies on standard benchmarks, including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. We highlight recurring trade-offs among effectiveness, efficiency, and evidence faithfulness, and conclude with open challenges for retrieval–reasoning agents, including structure-aware planning, transferable control policies, and robust stopping under distribution shift.

paper.title: SkillNav: A Multi-Agent Blackboard for Hallucination-Resistant Zero-Shot Object Navigation
paper.abstract: Embodied agents that route every high-level decision through a single language model typically ingest the entire trajectory at every step, a regime in which prompt context grows monotonically and both lost-in-the-middle degradation and trajectory-level hallucination peak. We show that multi-agent decoupling on a shared Voronoi-Frontier blackboard is a structural answer. SkillNav exposes a sparse topology over the partially-built map whose nodes carry visual evidence and two multiplicative gates (mu_safe, mu_mem) written by specialised Safe and Memory agents; a strategic Exploration agent reads only a compact, system-prompt-style summary of the blackboard – whose size is bounded by the topology rather than by trajectory length – and writes back only a phase decision plus an SR/IG weight pair. The three agents never see one another’s prompts; false-positive evidence is suppressed architecturally by mu_mem rather than by asking the language model to revise its own past output. On HM3D val, SkillNav reaches 71.9 SR / 34.0 SPL with only 22.5 LLM calls per episode (~11.9K total tokens), surpassing the strongest published zero-shot baseline (RATE-Nav) by +4.1 SR / +2.7 SPL.

paper.title: Riemannian Geometry for Pre-trained Language Model Embeddings
paper.abstract: Understanding the geometric structure of pre-trained language model embeddings matters for interpretability and safety. We ask whether sentence-level classification signal lives in the Riemannian geometry of contextual token embeddings, and probe it by extracting per-token pullback metrics from a learned encoder’s analytical Jacobian and aggregating them with the Frechet mean on the symmetric positive definite (SPD) manifold, we call this procedure Riemannian Mean Pooling (RMP). Across three datasets with non-trivial linguistic structure (CoLA, CREAK, RTE), RMP outperforms Euclidean mean pooling, while on FEVER-Symmetric, a benchmark constructed to remove annotation-driven lexical artifacts, the method correctly stays at chance. Ablations show that a randomly initialised encoder combined with Frechet aggregation already beats Euclidean pooling before any training, localising the source of the gain to the geometric aggregation rather than to learned manifold structure. The trained encoder adds a further 1.7 to 2.2 AUC points, consistently across the signal-bearing datasets rather than on any one of them.

paper.title: Trust but Verify: Introducing DAVinCI - A Framework for Dual Attribution and Verification in Claim Inference for Language Models
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency and versatility across a wide range of NLP tasks, yet they remain prone to factual inaccuracies and hallucinations. This limitation poses significant risks in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, and scientific communication, where trust and verifiability are paramount. In this paper, we introduce DAVinCI - a Dual Attribution and Verification framework designed to enhance the factual reliability and interpretability of LLM outputs. DAVinCI operates in two stages: (i) it attributes generated claims to internal model components and external sources; (ii) it verifies each claim using entailment-based reasoning and confidence calibration. We evaluate DAVinCI across multiple datasets, including FEVER and CLIMATE-FEVER, and compare its performance against standard verification-only baselines. Our results show that DAVinCI significantly improves classification accuracy, attribution precision, recall, and F1-score by 5-20%. Through an extensive ablation study, we isolate the contributions of evidence span selection, recalibration thresholds, and retrieval quality. We also release a modular DAVinCI implementation that can be integrated into existing LLM pipelines. By bridging attribution and verification, DAVinCI offers a scalable path to auditable, trustworthy AI systems. This work contributes to the growing effort to make LLMs not only powerful but also accountable. Our code is available at https://github.com/vr25/davinci.

paper.title: Semi-Supervised Learning to Improve Detection of Factual and Causal Errors in Language Models’ Explanations
paper.abstract: Language models (LMs) are increasingly used to generate decisions and explanations for high-stakes financial tasks, but these explanations can contain factual inconsistencies with the underlying claim or invalid causal reasoning. We propose a two-step auditing framework that decomposes each explanation into reasoning points and verifies them using natural language inference (NLI): (i) claim \Rightarrow point for factuality verification and (ii) point \Rightarrow conclusion for causality verification. To reduce reliance on expensive expert annotations, we study effective fine-tuning strategies based on semi-supervised learning (SSL) for NLI verifiers, leveraging abundant unlabeled explanations via pseudo-labeling and FreeMatch with self-adaptive confidence thresholds. Experiments across small language models and both encoder-only and decoder-only verifiers under varying labeling budgets show that SSL consistently outperforms the pre-trained baseline and supervised fine-tuning. FreeMatch is generally more robust than simple pseudo-labeling, suggesting better utilization of unlabeled data for scaling error detection of LMs’ generations.

paper.title: Is Safety Grounded or Detachable? Removal-Cost Audits for Open-Weight Language Models
paper.abstract: Open-weight language models remain modifiable after release, so release-time refusal alone cannot establish durable safety. We introduce removal-cost grounding as a budget-conditioned audit of whether safety can be weakened while preserving utility, coherent generation, and benign helpfulness. We formalize clean removal as a constrained feasibility problem and distinguish observed counterexamples from inconclusive attack searches. Mycelium v0 provides a deliberately limited case study: four model families exhibit benchmark degradation under an archived removal configuration, while targeted Mistral controls separate destructive ablation from wrapper bypass. A provenance audit excludes three model–task comparisons with mismatched evaluation limits or conflicting snapshots. Across the retained comparisons, mean removal-associated score changes range from -0.382 to -0.185. In a separate 12-prompt generation panel, the strict attack-success proxy increases from 1/12 with Mycelium enabled to 7/12 under bypass, with wide uncertainty and no matched native safety baseline. Adaptive traces further show why early-stopped checkpoints must be distinguished from training endpoints. These observations do not establish tamper-resistant safety. They motivate an auditable reporting framework in which the cheapest admissible route to useful unsafe behavior, rather than the costliest destructive ablation, determines the strength of a safety claim.

paper.title: CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20 to 33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5% of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, which indicates that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

paper.title: Grounding or Lexical Overlap? A Matched-Pair Study of Internals-Based Faithfulness Probes
paper.abstract: We provide a confound-controlled methodology and a released "wrong-question" diagnostic for internals-based, reference-free hallucination detection, which treats context-faithfulness (is an answer entailed by the context?) as a linear residual-stream direction. In the standard extractive setup, faithfulness is almost perfectly correlated with lexical overlap (r=0.99), so an apparent "grounding probe" may be a string-matching detector. Our matched Support×Overlap construction partially decouples the two (halving the confound to r=0.50), and the diagnostic fools an off-the-shelf NLI model. Across four instruction-tuned 7–9B families: (i) within the overlap-controlled stratum a support contrast is linearly decodable, but a no-context ablation shows it reflects question–answer compatibility rather than context use, and is inseparable from factoid-correctness by construction; (ii) it aligns across families up to a linear map, yet answer-length, overlap, and factuality directions align equally well, a generic matched-stimulus property, not grounding-specific; (iii) on the three families we could extract, the synthetic direction does not transfer to real hallucinations, scoring below NLI, confidence, and lexical overlap on RAGTruth, where only an in-domain probe trained on human labels recovers a usable signal.

paper.title: PARSE: Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization for Professional Domain LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Prompt injection defenses evaluated on synthetic benchmarks do not generalize to real enterprise documents, which are longer, denser, and interleave legitimate authority language with factual content. We demonstrate this gap with a benchmark of 122 tasks across five professional domains (financial, legal, medical, scientific, DevOps) built on real retrieved documents—actual SEC filings, Federal Register rules, PubMed abstracts, arXiv papers, and GitHub postmortems—paired with LLM-generated tasks and camouflaged payloads that were not human-validated. Paraphrasing, the strongest defense on synthetic benchmarks, shows no statistically significant attack success rate reduction on real documents (p=0.500) while degrading utility from 91.8% to 82.8%. We introduce PARSE (Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization), a domain-aware, fact-preserving sanitization pipeline that classifies each sentence by injection likelihood, extracts structured facts before rewriting, and verifies fact preservation via a consistency-checking loop. A directiveness gate routes 59% of real enterprise documents to a lightweight path, concentrating computational cost on high-risk documents. PARSE achieves 15.6% attack success rate—a 39% reduction versus the 25.4% baseline—at 86.9% utility, the largest reduction of any condition evaluated (h=−0.245), nominally significant (p=0.014) but not surviving correction for multiple comparisons. Practitioners should evaluate defenses on domain-matched real documents, not synthetic proxies.

paper.title: Does Quantization Erode Grounding? A Faithfulness Audit of On-Device LLM Compression
paper.abstract: Weight quantization is the default route to running language models on consumer hardware, yet its effect on contextual faithfulness—a model’s willingness to ground answers in provided context rather than memorized priors—remains untested: faithfulness benchmarks use full-precision models, and quantization studies measure accuracy and perplexity, not grounding. We audit two instruction-tuned 3B models (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B) across seven GGUF precisions from 16-bit to 2-bit, under aligned, counterfactual, and unanswerable contexts, using 300 SQuAD-derived items and three prompt templates per condition (900 trials per condition per precision). With an item-level clustered bootstrap we find faithfulness unchanged from 16 down to 5 bits in both models, while below that small but statistically detectable declines appear whose onset is model-dependent (4-bit for Llama, 3-bit for Qwen). Critically, production of the original, context-contradicting answer does not rise at any precision, so the intuitive "quantization erodes grounding" mechanism is not supported: lost faithfulness moves to off-target responses instead. Qwen additionally collapses into incoherent output at 2-bit while Llama stays fluent, making extreme compression a per-model question. Code and harness: https://github.com/movvaneeraj/quantfaith.

paper.title: The Citation-Faithfulness Illusion: Measuring Whether Grounded Answers Preserve Source Disagreement
paper.abstract: Grounding faithfulness is measured on two axes: whether the answer follows the retrieved context, and whether each claim is supported by the source it cites. Both can be satisfied in full by an answer that picks one side of a genuinely contested question, cites a source that holds that side, and drops the credible sources that disagree. We name this failure disagreement collapse, or the citation-faithfulness illusion, and treat it as a construct-validity hazard: a high citation score does not license the inference that the answer reflects the sources. Conflict-aware retrieval already prescribes reflecting credible debate; our contribution is to make that prescription measurable. We define disagreement recall and disagreement-attribution precision, both decoupled from answer correctness and conditioned on source credibility so that suppressing a debunked claim is not penalized; a five-component rubric with verbatim anchors; an annotation protocol for the credibility filter and for position identity; a matched-pair diagnostic that holds retrieval and citation availability fixed; and a pre-registered two-judge pilot with human adjudication. No empirical scores are reported; the contribution is the instrument and its frozen evaluation design.

paper.title: Lifecycle Faithfulness for Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Benchmarks, Evaluation, and the Vera-Life Controller
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation treats citation as a default proxy for reliability, yet a cited passage can support a claim and still be obsolete, superseded, contradicted, or invalid at the user’s target time. We name this failure a citation-supported lifecycle error and define lifecycle faithfulness: a claim-level criterion that requires semantic support, target-time validity, non-supersession, and provenance. We release Vera-Life-Eval, an 8,500-question benchmark with 41,203 versioned evidence pieces across six lifecycle settings (current, past, stale-only, update, conflict, and multi-hop), and Vera-Life, a low-training modular controller that builds an evidence-state graph, selects claim-evidence-time contracts, and chooses among answer, warn_stale, explain_conflict, retrieve_more, and abstain, emitting a claim-level lifecycle ledger. On a shared Qwen3-8B generator, Vera-Life raises LifeEM from .374 (best prompt-only baseline) to .623, and remains effective under timestamp-only (.584) and text-only (.504) regimes. Same-action controls, metadata isolation, and source-disjoint transfer across product, policy, scientific, and news evidence show that the gains are not an artefact of output format or Wikipedia revision cues. The next mission for RAG is not merely to cite evidence, but to know whether that evidence is still alive.

paper.title: Do LLM Attribution Metrics Transfer? Auditing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation Across Datasets and Constructs
paper.abstract: Practice often treats automatic metrics for attribution in LLM retrieval-augmented generation as interchangeable. We audit eight automatic scorers — lexical, embedding, and BERTScore baselines alongside entailment/grounding-trained models (clean and FEVER NLI, the checker MiniCheck) — across three evaluation constructs (provenance/topicality, generated-answer attribution, and fact-check entailment), asking whether any scorer transfers: stays within the 95% confidence interval of the best audited scorer on every dataset of a multi-dataset construct. In the construct with the most multi-dataset human-labeled coverage — generated-answer attribution (AttributionBench’s four source datasets, n = 1,610, with independent HAGRID, n = 2,150) — none of the audited automatic scorers does: the per-dataset metric rankings invert (Kendall τ = −0.64, p = 0.031 on AttributedQA vs. LFQA), and an off-the-shelf NLI scorer that is best on short-claim AttributedQA (AUROC 0.90) collapses to AUROC 0.53 (chance) on long-form LFQA, where BERTScore wins (0.91); the reversal persists under the tested truncation settings. This instability has a concrete decision cost: a naive "best-on-average" rule for choosing an evaluator fails leave-one-dataset-out (mean held-out regret 0.172 AUROC, worse than fixing one scorer), so metric choice should be validated on the target dataset rather than assumed from performance elsewhere. A prompt-based LLM judge avoids the chance-level collapses the automatic scorers suffer (no LFQA collapse) but is not uniformly best, ~100× costlier, and non-deterministic — relocating, not removing, the validation burden.

paper.title: EviScope: Paired Counterfactual Evidence Diagnostics for Faithful and Efficient Grounded Language Models
paper.abstract: Grounded language-model systems are often evaluated by final answer accuracy, yet a correct answer can be unsupported, drawn from the wrong source, or produced when evidence is insufficient or contradictory. We introduce EviScope, a paired counterfactual benchmark that holds the question fixed while adding, removing, distracting, or contradicting its evidence. EviScope-v1.1 contains 40 four-condition quartets with repaired counterfactual claims and span-level support labels for automatic evaluation. Across 960 gold-blind generations from Qwen2.5-7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, paired metrics expose model-dependent grounding behavior that answer accuracy hides. On two local open models, an explicit evidence-action gate underperforms vanilla RAG on QCS: 0.15 vs. 0.50 for Qwen and 0.10 vs. 0.375 for Llama. Gemini reaches 0.944 joint success under both prompts, yet still answers 5% of conflict cases after contradiction insertion. EviScope therefore distinguishes unsupported answering, conflict blindness, and wrong non-answer actions rather than scoring answers alone.

paper.title: Does RAG Know When Retrieval Is Wrong? Diagnosing Context Compliance under Knowledge Conflict
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is usually evaluated by whether the final answer is correct. Under knowledge conflict, this hides a key question: did the model follow retrieved evidence, rely on its parametric prior, or produce a post-hoc rationale? We study this as context compliance, the regime in which retrieved context controls the answer even when it conflicts with the model’s prior knowledge. We introduce Context-Driven Decomposition (CDD), an inference-time diagnostic intervention that elicits contextual and prior answers, isolates the conflicting premise, and records a resolution trace that can be perturbed. Across Epi-Scale stress tests, TruthfulQA misconception injection, and cross-model reruns, CDD makes three behaviors visible. First, misleading retrieval can severely degrade accuracy: under worst-case injected context (a TruthfulQA misconception-injection probe), Standard RAG reaches only 15.0%. Second, better answers need not share the same mechanism: CDD improves adversarial accuracy on Gemini-2.5-Flash and shows directional gains across Claude variants, yet trace-perturbation sensitivity is high only on Gemini. Third, explicit decomposition improves controlled-conflict robustness over a conflict-aware instruction baseline on localized factual conflicts, with the clearest margins on Entity Swap (88.0% vs 79.3%) and Logical Contradiction (83.2% vs 75.4%). We frame RAG conflict handling as an observability problem.

paper.title: Self-Detect–Refine: Iterative Training Label Refinement Method for Clinical Note Generation
paper.abstract: In medical LLM adaptation, collecting large-scale real clinical notes is constrained by patient privacy and annotation cost, so training pipelines often rely on notes synthesized by commercial LLMs. Those synthetic notes are not error-free. We observe that after fine-tuning on such notes, a task judge rates the resulting model’s outputs as more complete without a consistent Accuracy gain, while a hallucination judge flags more statements that the source does not support. We therefore report Accuracy and Completeness separately from hallucination counts, split the latter into Content and Format-Meta hallucinations, and report both as rates normalized by the number of fields each output format requires, so that a gain in one cannot hide a loss in the other. We then introduce Self-Detect–Refine, which applies an external LLM to detect and revise hallucinations in the training labels themselves rather than in outputs at inference time. We evaluate it across three base models, two refiners, and four refinement depths, fine-tuning a fresh copy of each base model on each label snapshot. GPT-5.2-refined labels lower Content hallucinations in every configuration, both as a share of the required fields and after length normalization. The two stages load on different components: the Completeness gain belongs to raw-label fine-tuning, whereas refinement raises Accuracy without a consistent loss in Completeness. Format-Meta changes are mixed, a lower-cost refiner is less consistent, and every judgment here comes from LLM judges on a single synthetic benchmark without clinician validation.

paper.title: Graph Evidence Is Not Text Evidence: Serialization Faithfulness as Structural Invariance in Graph-Grounded Language Models
paper.abstract: Graph-grounded language models are usually evaluated by answer accuracy, yet a serialized prompt is a string representation of a graph rather than the graph itself. We argue that faithful graph-grounded reasoning requires the composed predictor F_\theta \circ z to be well-defined on graph-query equivalence classes: structurally equivalent graph-query pairs should induce the same prediction regardless of textual realization. We formalize this as a structural invariance property, decompose unfaithfulness into syntactic instability, semantic interference, and distractor susceptibility, and introduce corresponding diagnostics. On controlled graph reasoning tasks, DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves 98.9% accuracy and near-perfect syntactic stability (FS = .975), yet its isomorphism consistency drops from .969 to .701 under semantic-name relabeling (∆_{sem} = .268); only 72.9% of originally correct answers survive this transformation. Across four model families, we observe targeted semantic interference in high-accuracy models, broad unfaithfulness in weaker models, and near-perfect invariance as a capability ceiling. A graph-grounded LLM can be accurate without being structurally faithful: its predictions may fail to remain invariant under graph-equivalent textual relabelings.

paper.title: CoSched-Cert: Faithful Multi-Turn Scheduling Dialogue via Solver-Verified Certificates
paper.abstract: Multi-turn scheduling assistants must preserve constraint edits and distinguish solver evidence from language-model interpretations. We present CoSched-Cert, a dialogue protocol combining a typed scheduling language, solver-distinguishing clarification, cost-based conflict localization, verified repair synthesis, and lexical certificate auditing. Its guarantees are conditional on the encoded problem and supplied candidate interpretations; lexical support does not establish semantic entailment. SchedNL-Bench-Cert contains 1,000 synthetic Chinese/English utterances and 350 sessions. Gold-AST replay measures internal consistency against labels generated by the same engine, while author-written protocol simulations illustrate selected design choices. Across three live-parser seeds on 52 sessions, session training and registered sibling augmentation raise conditional micro target-constraint agreement from 18.0% to 83.7%. The final configuration has 100% coarse status agreement but only 75.0% conflict-member agreement, and includes a rule informed by a test-session failure. We therefore treat these results as descriptive, not as an unbiased generalization estimate. We define a stricter joint-turn criterion and report the bounds supported by the available aggregates. The contribution is a protocol for exposing inspectable solver evidence and the remaining gap between encoded feasibility and user-intent correctness.

paper.title: The Citation Expansion Trap: Operating-Point Control for Fixed-Answer Multi-Hop RAG Citation Repair
paper.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation systems often produce answers with incomplete or noisy citation sets. When the answer text is fixed, citation repair may seem to require only adding retrieved evidence. We show that this view is incomplete: in multi-hop settings, expansion that recovers missing support can also introduce plausible distractors into the evidence bundle. We study fixed-answer citation-set repair as a diagnostic protocol for reporting policies as operating points between support-ID coverage and distractor control. Across a calibrated 5,000-example HotpotQA diagnostic and Qwen2.5-generated outputs on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2Wiki, cross-encoder repair yields cleaner support-ID operating points than BM25 expansion on HotpotQA and 2Wiki, while MuSiQue shifts the policy into a higher-distractor-cost regime under harder compositional transfer. We do not claim universal transfer of absolute performance from HotpotQA alone; the cross-dataset pattern is instead consistent with mechanism-level transfer of the support-distractor operating-point geometry. A single-author audit of 450 unique generated-output cases plus 60 duplicate checks reinforces this caution: support-ID coverage and claim-level citation support can diverge. We therefore recommend an operating-point scorecard for citation repair and separate support-ID diagnostics from stronger claim-level faithfulness claims.

paper.title: Staged Linguistic Seeding: Grounded Query Expansion for Verified-Unit QA in AI Contact Centers
paper.abstract: Customer-service QA in an AI contact center (AICC) runs under deployment constraints that benchmark QA misses: tight voice-hotline latency and a high cost for unsupported or wrong automatic answers. We deploy a system that answers only from a closed set of verified QA units: it returns a retrieved unit verbatim, or routes to clarify/abstain/handoff.The index is enriched offline by staged linguistic seeding (SLS): a human authors a per-unit world-grounded slot recipe, gpt-4.1-mini renders it into variants, and a light human gate filters them, one methodology reused across both domains, so inference stays a single retrieval pass with no query-time generation.On held-out query variants (in-distribution recipe reformulations) from two industrial domains, SLS is the dominant retrieval lever, lifting hybrid R@1 to 0.881/0.930 (+0.27/+0.34); the gain holds across all five retrievers we test. The win is the design, not the volume: at the same gpt-4.1-mini, SLS beats a budget-matched doc2query by +0.20/+0.32, and a cross-provenance control provides additional evidence of transfer across generated-query distributions; the embedding choice is secondary. Verified-unit answering also removes free-form generation’s unsupported-content surface (7–13% vs. ≈0%). We report this as an honest application study, including negative results.

paper.title: Structured Pruning and Lightweight Adaptation of Foundation Models for Resource-Efficient Earth Observation
paper.abstract: Structured pruning has gained attention as a promising solution for the cost-effective deployment of large language, vision-language, and domain-specific foundation models. However, most prior work has focused on general-purpose language models and often lacks a systematic comparison of pruning strategies across model scales, architectures, and real-world multimodal applications. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of structured pruning methods, focusing on depth pruning, width pruning, and post-pruning recovery with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We evaluate multiple open-source models, including Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, LLaVA-OneVision-0.5B, and Phi-4-Mini-Instruct, across intrinsic metrics and downstream benchmarks such as BBH, MATH Hard, MuSR, and MMLU-Pro. Our findings reveal that (1) depth pruning generally provides a more stable trade-off between efficiency and performance than width pruning; (2) width pruning can reduce memory usage, but often gives limited throughput gains and less predictable accuracy retention; (3) reasoning-intensive benchmarks, particularly mathematical reasoning tasks, are more sensitive to structured pruning than some other evaluation tasks; (4) LoRA-based post-pruning adaptation can substantially recover performance after moderate pruning; and (5) pruning behaviors observed in general-purpose models transfer to Earth observation foundation models, as demonstrated on TerraMind, where depth pruning reduces latency and GPU memory usage while maintaining competitive EuroSAT and Bigearthnet task accuracy.

paper.title: E-SENS: Exclusion-Sensitive Penalization for Negative-Constraint Retrieval
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models can fail to respect negative constraints when the retriever supplies evidence about concepts the user explicitly excluded. Beyond explicit negation, queries may ask for answers that include one concept while excluding another, or for entities that belong to a category but differ from a closely related instance. Because the excluded concept still appears in the query text, dense retrievers may assign high similarity to documents about that concept even when the user asks to avoid it. We introduce E-SENS, a training-free reranking method for negation-sensitive retrieval. E-SENS extracts a compact trap query for the excluded side and subtracts trap-query similarity from the original-query retrieval score. On ExcluIR, E-SENS shows a clear recall-violation trade-off across four embedding models and reduces trap retrieval at recall-preserving settings.

paper.title: How Far Can You Get Without a GPU? A Systematic Benchmark of Lightweight Hallucination Detection Across Question Answering, Dialogue, and Summarisation
paper.abstract: Hallucination detection has become a pressing requirement for trustworthy AI deployment at scale. The most accurate detection methods depend on GPU-intensive inference, proprietary API calls, or white-box access to the generating model. This puts them out of reach for resource-constrained researchers and practitioners. In this paper, we explore a practical alternative: how well can hallucination detection perform using only lightweight, CPU-feasible methods built on publicly available models? We systematically benchmark four such detectors, ROUGE-L, semantic similarity, BERTScore, and a Natural Language Inference (NLI) detector based on a FEVER-trained DeBERTa model, together with a score-level ensemble of similarity and NLI. We evaluate them across all three tasks of the HaluEval benchmark: question answering (QA), dialogue, and summarisation. We calibrate each method on a held-out validation split and evaluate it on 2,000 test instances per task, and we report bootstrap confidence intervals for the main results. We find that the similarity-NLI ensemble is the most consistent method, but that absolute performance is highly task-dependent. The ensemble ranks best on QA (F1 = 0.792, AUC-ROC = 0.873) and on dialogue (F1 = 0.694, AUC-ROC = 0.749), where NLI is the strongest standalone method; on summarisation every method performs near chance (AUC-ROC between 0.469 and 0.574). We then ask whether that failure is intrinsic to lightweight detection or an artifact of our single-pass design, and find it is largely the latter. Raising the premise budget from 800 to 1600 characters lifts summarisation AUC-ROC from 0.567 to 0.629, and replacing single-pass scoring with sentence-level chunk aggregation reaches 0.683, still on CPU and with the same model, though at roughly twenty times the NLI inference. Summarisation remains by far the hardest task, but our results do not support treating lightweight detection as intrinsically unsuited to it. All experiments run on a standard laptop CPU using public models.

paper.title: Memory Makes the Difference: Evaluating How Different Memory Roles Shape Conversational Agents
paper.abstract: Memory is a critical component of modern conversational systems. Prior research on memory mechanisms in RAG-based conversational systems has focused on how memory is stored and retrieved. However, less is known about how memories with different functional roles influence response quality, shape agents’ responses across conversational contexts, and lead to distinct response behaviors. Existing evaluations are also largely reference-based, often missing response nuances that address users’ preferences differently. In this work, we study the impact of different memory types on agent responses. We present a fine-grained taxonomy of conversational memory, classify retrieved memories by functional role, and design a user-centric evaluation framework that simulates user perspectives. Through comparative experiments on long-term datasets and frontier LLMs, our analysis reveals differentiated effects of memory: e.g., clarifying memory is associated with improved factual accuracy and constraint awareness, making responses more correct and personalized, while irrelevant memory reduces topic relevance and degrades constraint awareness. These findings show that, despite the power of frontier LLMs, different memory types can be leveraged to produce responses better aligned with a user’s stated constraints, and motivate further research in this direction.

paper.title: Relational Grounding Failures in Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Dialogue Summarization with Small Language Models
paper.abstract: We diagnose relational grounding failures in zero-shot English-to-Chinese dialogue summarization with small language models (SLMs). We develop and apply a Dialogue-Semantic Grounding Error Taxonomy to evaluate three open-weight SLMs alongside a supervised mBART baseline. The taxonomy captures errors in entities, events, speaker roles, circumstances, modality, discourse outcomes, omissions, and language or format issues. Our analysis shows that SLM hallucinations often involve relation-sensitive distortions of dialogue-relevant content: models may preserve source-relevant participants, events, or circumstances while altering who did what, under what conditions, or with what outcome. These findings position the taxonomy as a diagnostic evaluation framework for dialogue summarization, revealing relation-sensitive faithfulness failures that reference-based metrics may obscure.

paper.title: A Randomization-Control Diagnostic for Document Grounding in Self-Distillation Gates
paper.abstract: Self-distillation for grounded question answering often filters tutor trajectories with agreement or confidence gates. For such gates to support faithful grounding, their signals should depend on the supplied document rather than on answers recoverable from parametric memory. We propose a four-mode randomization-control diagnostic that applies the same frozen gate to original, randomized, irrelevant, and empty documents for the same question. On HotpotQA and MuSiQue, using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with eight tutor traces, the joint gate changes sharply with document condition: kept fraction falls from 0.380 to 0.020 and from 0.330 to 0.015, respectively. Randomized and irrelevant documents lie between the endpoints, while a document-blind random gate stays flat. The protocol audits document sensitivity without additional student training; faithful evidence use and downstream gains require separate validation.

paper.title: Safe Adaptive Context and TACER: Task-Aware Evidence Routing for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines often pass a fixed number of retrieved documents to the generator, even though evidence needs vary by query. We study context selection as a post-retrieval control problem: given the same candidate list, how much evidence should enter the prompt, and in what form? We present Safe Adaptive Context, a lightweight controller that starts with limited evidence and expands when the generated answer appears weak, and TACER, a task-aware extension that routes between compact evidence and safer broader context using retrieval-side and evidence-coverage signals. Across five datasets, two generators, and stronger retriever settings, the controllers substantially reduce provider-reported token use while preserving most Fixed Top-10 answer quality. In a five-dataset, 500-query external-baseline stress test, Safe Adaptive Context retains 99.8% of Fixed Top-10 F1 with 55.0% token reduction, while TACER retains 99.4% with 60.4% token reduction. The contribution is not universal quality improvement, but practical quality-preserving efficiency through task-aware context control.

paper.title: When Should an Agent Distrust Its Own Context? Model-Dependent Outcomes of an Audited Reasoning Pipeline
paper.abstract: Agents grounded in heterogeneous sources often encounter conflicting evidence. We study an Audited Reasoning Pipeline (ARP): a forensic analyzer reads the raw sources and emits a sanitized diagnostic, while a clean-room synthesis stage receives the question and diagnostic but not the raw context. On 100 corrupted ConflictQA instances per model, ARP raises exact match from 15 to 30 for GPT-OSS-120B and from 19 to 29 for MiniMax-M2.5.CAT-Source changes from 40 to 49 and from 74 to 56, respectively; their paired model-by-condition interaction is 27 points (95% CI [13,41], p < .001), although two model/configuration pairs do not identify capability as its cause. The three diagnostic metrics are emitted before the clean-room boundary, and all items are corrupted, so conflict detection has no false-positive evaluation. Token-F1 also falls on multi-answer questions. Because the clean four-call control that gives Stage 4 both raw context and the diagnostic was not run, the air- gap’s causal effect remains unidentified.

paper.title: What Does Answer Change Rate Actually Measure? A Specificity Audit of Causal Intervention Tests for Explanation Faithfulness

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Information Technology Dharwad

paper.abstract: A growing line of work tests whether large language model (LLM) explanations are faithful by intervening on the explanation (removing, perturbing, or swapping it) and checking whether the model’s final answer changes – an Answer Change Rate (ACR), read as causal evidence. We argue this inference requires a control existing work has not consistently reported: whether the answer changes comparably under an unrelated disturbance. We run the causal intervention paradigm on 12 models (6 matched base/instruction-tuned pairs, 8B–70B parameters) on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM, adding a content-free filler control matched for length, a re-injection baseline measuring re-prompting and decoding instability, and paired significance testing across conditions. McNemar’s test does not detect a significantly larger answer-change rate for removal than for the control in 14 of 24 model–task cells (58%) – an absence of detected difference, not equivalence – the re-prompting/decoding floor alone exceeds 80% answer-change in one model, and a commonly assumed instruction-tuning effect does not replicate across families. We do not conclude that LLM explanations are faithful or unfaithful; we conclude that ACR frequently fails a basic specificity check and cannot alone support causal-faithfulness claims. We release the full pipeline and propose a minimal reporting standard for future studies.

paper.title: Gradient-Aligned Iterative Fine-Tuning for Adaptive LLM Post-Training
paper.abstract: Post-training has become the primary mechanism for grounding large language models (LLMs) to application-specific domains, enabling them to acquire new knowledge, behaviors, and policies beyond pre-training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization are the dominant paradigms for this adaptation, but are typically applied sequentially, requiring careful tuning of training schedules, regularization, and other hyperparameters.We propose Gradient-Aligned Iterative Fine-Tuning (GAIF), an adaptive post-training framework that combines three complementary components: a unified SFT+DPO objective optimized simultaneously; a prospective adaptive weighting mechanism that selects task weights based on next-step gradient geometry; and an iterative outer loop that regenerates preference pairs from the current model’s failures, keeping the supervision signal synchronized with the model’s evolving capabilities while adapting training toward arbitrary evaluation metrics, including non-differentiable ones.We evaluate GAIF on a production-scale generative movie search assistant, where a 7B LLM is adapted to the entertainment domain while remaining faithful to a fixed streaming catalog. The 7B model trained with GAIF outperforms standard SFT, sequential SFT+DPO, and a ~90B reference model in both ranking quality (NDCG) and output validity. Experiments on GSM8K mathematical reasoning further show the algorithm’s effectiveness extends beyond grounded retrieval.

paper.title: Geometry-Conditioned Turn Scoring for Conversational Memory Compression
paper.abstract: Compressing long multi-turn conversations requires deciding not only how to compress context, but which signal should rank memory candidates under a fixed budget. We study a sparse keep/compress/drop (KCD) codec and compare geometric, semantic, and hybrid scoring signals across conversational memory regimes. On a stress-test benchmark designed to expose support-turn failures, a geometry-scored codec substantially outperforms a semantic signal swap inside the same codec. On MSC (1,000 conversations), we show that geometry-based compression methods substantially outperform LongLLMLingua on geometric fidelity (ΔL2 ≈ +130) while LongLLMLingua modestly improves answer NLL—a geometry-behavior divergence confirming that behavioral metrics alone are insufficient to evaluate memory compression. Among KCD signal variants on MSC (1,000 conversations, Qwen2.5-1.5B), query-conditioned geometry achieves the best combination of geometric fidelity and behavioral quality simultaneously: at budget 0.50 it reduces logit L2 by 109.4 units versus semantic KCD (p<0.001, conversation-level) while also achieving best answer NLL across all budgets. On LongMemEval-S (100 full-length conversations), all KCD variants significantly improve behavioral quality over uniform compression. A Llama-3.2-3B cross-model check shows that the geometry signal advantage is model-family-dependent: semantic compression dominates geometry compression on behavior across all budgets for Llama-3B (p≤0.01, conversation-level). The paper’s central claim is that geometry-behavior divergence is real and consequential, and that query-conditioned geometry is the signal that best resolves it on Qwen2.5 models.

paper.title: Faithfulness Is Not Free: Auditing Offline KV-Cache Quantization in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

author.affiliation: National University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can precompute and store key-value (KV) caches of retrieved documents to avoid re-encoding the same context for every query. Quantizing these offline caches reduces storage cost, but existing work largely evaluates compression through accuracy alone and does not ask whether the generated answers remain faithful to the retrieved evidence. This distinction is important because a model can preserve the correct answer string while weakening its grounding in the provided context. We audit Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under BF16, INT8, and INT4 offline KV-cache settings on RGB and HotpotQA, measuring both answer accuracy and faithfulness using a hallucination detector, NLI entailment, and an LLM judge. INT8 is nearly lossless across accuracy and faithfulness metrics. In contrast, INT4 reduces accuracy and, more critically, degrades faithfulness even on examples where the answer remains factually correct: over 90% of faithfulness flips are negative. The degradation increases under noisier retrieval and larger retrieval depth. These results show that compressed RAG systems cannot be validated by EM or F1 alone; faithfulness must be audited before low-bit offline KV caches are deployed.

paper.title: Cross-Modal Grounding for Calibrated Confidence in Vision Language Models

author.affiliation: United States Military Academy at West Point
Pathfinder Applied Research, LLC, Syracuse University, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and Johns Hopkins University

paper.abstract: We introduce a novel approach for calibrating uncertainty quantification (UQ) tailored for visual language models (VLMs). Existing state-of-the-art UQ methods rely on consistency among multiple responses, but often report higher confidence when the model is consistently incorrect, leading to poorly calibrated confidence. To address this, we leverage cross-modal consistency by grounding back the textual responses to visual inputs. The confidence from the grounding model (GM) is used to calibrate the overall confidence. Given that using a GM adds its own uncertainty, we apply temperature scaling to calibrate the GM’s confidence in the accuracy of the generated responses. We comprehensively evaluate the proposed approach across diverse range of settings, including datasets with varying visuo-linguistic complexity, Q&A and caption generation tasks, general visual and specialized medical contexts, VLMs differing in scale, openness, and different categories of GMs. Experimental results show that our approach consistently improves confidence calibration, with expected calibration error (ECE) improvements ranging from 32.5% to 96.7% over both self and non-self consistency-based baselines. Code is available here https://github.com/trilokpadhi/Multimodal-Uncertainty-Quantification.

paper.title: Lost In Translation: Uneven Grounding Degradation Under Cross-Lingual Shift in LLM-Assisted Cyber Threat Intelligence
paper.abstract: We introduce CrossCTI, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounding faithfulness in open-source large language models applied to cyber threat intelligence (CTI) analysis. Existing CTI and forensic NLP benchmarks are predominantly English-centric, leaving a critical gap in understanding how grounding faithfulness degrades under cross-lingual distribution shift, a realistic condition in multinational security operations centers. CrossCTI translates 50 English CTI reports into Arabic, Chinese, Swahili, and Russian using NLLB-200 with entity-preserving masking, achieving 100% IOC preservation across languages. We construct 26 forensic question-answer pairs and evaluate each against all five language corpora and three open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3), producing 390 evaluation instances, scored with token-level F1, character-level F1, and entailment-based attribution. Using a repeated-measures mixed-effects analysis that accounts for the fact that each of the 26 items is evaluated under all 15 model\timeslanguage conditions, we find that cross-lingual degradation is severe, but uneven across metrics: language is the dominant, robust predictor of lexical (token-level) grounding quality (p<0.001), with no detectable effect of model identity on this metric. In contrast, model identity is a significant predictor of both character-level overlap and entailment-based attribution (p<0.01), including a specific interaction in one model (Mistral) that underperforms specifically in Swahili. Token-level F1 drops from 0.44 (English) to 0.03 (Arabic); gold-chunk retrieval recall drops from 0.962 (English) to 0.115 (Arabic); and the instance-level correlation between retrieval success and token-level grounding is r=0.60. Performance also improves from the top-k=1 to the top-k=3 retrieved passages before plateauing, with no consistent gains from the additional retrieved content. We further show that the entailment-based attribution metric is significantly elevated specifically for the model used to generate the benchmark’s own QA pairs, a synthetic-annotator confound that we quantify directly via within-item paired tests rather than only disclosing qualitatively. CrossCTI provides a reproducible framework for multilingual CTI grounding evaluation and a case study in how the apparent dominant factor, language or model, depends on which grounding metric is used.

paper.title: RuleChef: Grounding LLM Task Knowledge in Human-Editable Rules

author.affiliation: KR Labs, Technische Universität Wien and Technical University of Budapest
TU Wien Institute for Information Systems Engineering

paper.abstract: We present RuleChef, a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate executable rules for NLP tasks such as text classification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), or relation extraction. Rules are generated based on a task description and a set of labeled examples, then they are iteratively improved based both on additional examples and on human feedback over existing rules. RuleChef can also be used to bootstrap rules using the observed input-output pairs from any existing model for a given task. LLMs are used only at learning time, synthesizing rules and iteratively patching them based on failures measured on a held-out split. The result of this process is a fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule system. Preliminary evaluation is performed on both classification and NER tasks. We release RuleChef as open-source software under an Apache 2.0 license.

paper.title: Compression-Aware Abstention: Teaching LLMs to Refuse When KV-Compression Masks Remove Answer Evidence
paper.abstract: KV-cache compression reduces LLM inference memory by evicting context tokens, but when the evicted tokens contain answer-bearing evidence, the model may hallucinate instead of recognizing that the compressed context is insufficient. We address this failure from a behavioral perspective: to our knowledge, this is the first work to formulate compression-aware abstention as a learning problem, in which a model learns to answer when supporting evidence survives compression and abstain when it does not. We construct supervision from compressor survival masks and tight answer-bearing spans, labeling examples as Confident when evidence survives and Abstain when it is removed. A 10.1M-parameter LoRA adapter trained on ∼2.6K MuSiQue 2-hop QA examples reduces base-model hallucinations by 97% under prompt-style truncation while preserving correct answering on evidence-retaining examples. Unlike prompt-only abstention baselines, which over-abstain on many answerable high-retention examples, the trained adapter learns a conditional policy. We also evaluate the method under actual compressed-cache decoding, where multi-compressor training yields a 6–22× relative lift over the unaided base on evidence-retaining examples. Controlled-deletion experiments show that the learned behavior is driven by evidence content rather than input length alone.

paper.title: Eval-Pair Matrix: Answer-Paired Meta-Evaluation of LLM Judges for Grounded RAG
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is widely used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but reusing a model as generator and judge complicates identifying self-leniency. We introduce Eval-Pair Matrix, a controlled meta-evaluation protocol for source-grounded RAG. Starting from GaRAGe, we induce one hidden answer-causal contradiction per record, generate answers from perturbed passages with GPT, Grok, and Gemini, and use the same models as blind judges against the original passages. The experiment contains 300 core records, 897 labeled outputs, and 2,683 verdicts in a crossed 3×3 matrix; the primary analysis uses 275 validated records. We estimate same-model effects by pairing judges on the exact same candidate answer. Diagonal and off-diagonal F1 are similar, and aggregate paired recall is near zero for the three tested endpoints (−0.5 pp; 95% cluster-bootstrap CI [−2.7,+1.7]). Matching judges flag answers that avoided the induced claim less often (−4.3 pp). A targeted human evaluation classifies reviewed apparent false positives as alternate source-error detections, adoption-label mistakes, or unclear cases; none were adjudicated as genuine false alarms. We recommend full matrices, answer-paired effects, behavior strata, and label-task alignment.

paper.title: Beyond Document Grounding: Span-Level Hallucination Detection over Code, Tool Output, and Documents

author.affiliation: KR Labs, Technische Universität Wien and Technical University of Budapest
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and McGill University
TU Wien Institute for Information Systems Engineering

paper.abstract: Hallucination detection for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is usually evaluated on natural-language document evidence. However, grounded generation systems increasingly rely on structured inputs: source code, developer-tool output, markdown documents, tables, and repository metadata. We introduce a unified benchmark for span-level hallucination detection over code, tool output, structured documents, and existing natural-language RAG datasets. The benchmark is built by starting from grounded correct answers, injecting localized hallucinations with exact character labels, and validating the code test split with evidence-based review. Our fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B detector reaches 0.689 span-F1 on the unified test set and 0.60 on the code-agent source, where it substantially outperforms LettuceDetect-large (0.17) and the strongest zero-shot LLM judges we evaluated (at most 0.22). The same model remains competitive on established natural-language benchmarks, with 81.8 RAGTruth example-F1 and 0.724 English PsiloQA IoU.

paper.title: Does Retrieval Augmented Generation Collapse When It Retrieves AI-Generated Documents?

author.affiliation: University of Massachusetts at Amherst and University of Massachusetts at Amherst

paper.abstract: AI-generated text now constitutes a substantial and growing fraction of indexed web content, creating a feedback loop in which AI assistants may retrieve and condition on their own prior generations. Prior work shows that recursive training on model generations causes model collapse: a loss of output diversity and distributional drift. We ask whether a similar collapse emerges at inference time, when LLMs retrieve their own generations via RAG without any parameter updates. We measure collapse as the progressive convergence of responses to a narrow set across recursive retrieval rounds. Across three contamination simulations and four open-source LLMs, answer collapse is rapid and consistent under direct contamination, but slower, partial, and model-dependent under realistic competitive retrieval. Collapse can also degrade downstream accuracy on factual multi-hop QA, though the effect is inconsistent across models. We further show that the self-generated documents we introduce are cited far above their share of the retrieved context, an effect that is not fully explained by document quality, writing style, AI authorship, and self-preference. Finally, we propose and evaluate mitigation strategies at both the retrieval and generation stages, none of which reliably prevent collapse. As AI-generated content continues to populate the open web, collapse-resistant retrieval design becomes a prerequisite for trustworthy AI assistants.

paper.title: Similar Accuracy, Unequal Evidence: Search APIs as Decision Surfaces for Tool-Using Agents
paper.abstract: Search APIs expose ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata on which agents decide whether to answer, search again, or fetch pages. We evaluate these interfaces as decision surfaces on a fixed sample of 100 questions from the 254-question SEALQA-HARD subset, using one frozen GPT-5.4 agent, a fixed orchestration harness, and a shared page-fetch backend across Brave, Tavily, and Firecrawl. A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labels visible URL-level evidence;a separate answer audit yields 25, 25, and 26 correct answers out of 100. These counts indicate similar observed accuracy but do not establish equivalence. Under the tested configurations, Brave exposes more pre-fetch support alongside a larger snippet surface; Tavily has a larger rank-1 share among trajectory-pooled supporting observations; and Firecrawl is associated with broader exploration. First-search query-level metrics distinguish support availability from ranking, while contradiction exposure complements contradiction-to-gold ratios. A retrospective oracle union covers 44/100 questions, versus 26/100 for the best individual provider: 18 percentage points of headroom. The observed evidence and action differences motivate evaluating search APIs jointly with agent policy and retrieval budget.

paper.title: Latent Truth Decoding: Training Free Mitigation of Sycophancy in Small Language Models
paper.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) under 10B parameters are increasingly deployed on edge devices for privacy-sensitive, latency-critical applications, where their factual reliability is pivotal and no larger model is available to fall back on. These SLMs frequently exhibit sycophancy: they abandon a correct answer the moment a user confidently asserts an incorrect one. In this paper, we study where this failure originates and how to fix it without retraining. We introduce a prefix/suffix multiple-choice construction that reduces every question to a single answer token, enabling layer-wise analysis of exactly when a model commits to the truth or the lie. Using this probe, we show that sycophancy is pervasive and, crucially, that it is a routing failure rather than a knowledge failure, i.e. middle layers retrieve the correct answer with a strong, linearly separable signal but the final alignment layers route the residual stream away from it. We also show that this behaviour is seen far more in procedural reasoning, where the SLM has to think in a step-by-step fashion, than in factual recall, where the answer depends heavily on pretraining information. We quantify this with a layer-wise Criticality Score and localize the suppression to a narrow band of late layers. Building on this, we propose Latent Truth Decoding (LTD), a training-free intervention that decodes from the model’s epistemic peak rather than its final layer.

paper.title: Stable Scores, Failed Retrieval: Diagnosing RAG Evaluation in Low-Resource Indic Languages
paper.abstract: Automatic metrics stand in for native-speaker evaluation in low-resource retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so their validity determines what can be concluded about these systems. We test whether common metrics detect re- trieval and grounding failure in one fixed RAG pipeline across ten Indic languages. They do not merely miss the failure in Santali; they invert it. Hit@5 is 0.011, yet raw XLM-R BERTScore is the highest in the set at 0.902, changes little when retrieved evidence is re- moved, and assigns nearly the same score to matched and unrelated references. The cause is coverage: the scorer maps 39% of Santali tokens to <unk>, and a scorer whose vocab- ulary includes Ol Chiki restores discrimina- tion while LaBSE does not. Retrieval fails for the same reason. The gold article is indexed for 80% of Santali queries, but the retriever shares XLM-R’s tokenizer and collapses before reranking. Judge-based faithfulness and con- text precision, computed by a model with a dif- ferent tokenizer, flag the failure independently. A metric that cannot represent a script does not become noisy; it becomes constant and high. We argue that metric validity in low-resource languages must be established per language, and that evidence removal, reference shuffling, and the scorer’s <unk> rate can be important additions.

paper.title: Skip One Layer? A Multilingual and Multi-Task Study of Single-Layer Skipping in Modern Language Models

author.affiliation: Institut Teknologi Bandung and Institut Teknologi Bandung

paper.abstract: Modern language models are typically deployed using all transformer layers during inference, implicitly assuming that every layer contributes positively to downstream performance. Prior studies on layer skipping often focus on limited settings and commonly associate removable layers with specific transformer regions, particularly middle layers. However, whether single-layer skipping generalizes across diverse tasks, languages, and model architectures remains underexplored.In this work, we conduct a multilingual and multi-task empirical study of single-layer skipping in modern instruct-tuned language models. We evaluate 9 text-only models spanning multiple model families and parameter scales, including Gemma 3, Llama 3.2, and Qwen 3, OLMo 2 without modifying model parameters. Our experiments systematically evaluate single-layer skipping across all layers on diverse benchmarks covering NLU, reasoning, bias evaluation, code generation, instruction following, and multilingual knowledge evaluation, including MMLU across 57 subject domains and 10 typologically diverse languages.Our results show that the effect of single-layer skipping is highly context-dependent. We show that skipping a single transformer layer is an effective strategy for leveraging the capabilities of a language model: there is a high chance of achieving better benchmark performance while simultaneously reducing computation during inference. However, the optimal skipped layer varies depending on model architecture, task, domain, and language. Beneficial skipped layers occur most frequently in the second half of the network, though they also emerge in early layers in some cases. We further observe that performance improvements are more common in structured prediction tasks, whereas degradations more frequently occur in tasks requiring precise generation.

paper.title: Quality-Aware LLM Data Augmentation for Arabic Dialectal NER
paper.abstract: Named Entity Recognition for dialectal Arabic remains severely constrained by data scarcity, and LLM-based augmentation is the natural remedy. We study LLM-based augmentation for the Lebanese and Palestinian sub-corpora of Wojood 2024, using LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct as a generation backbone, and compare three strategies (entity-level, context-level, combined) across two k-shot sampling paradigms. The proposed multi-dimensional pipeline yields a per-sentence composite score Q(s) that exposes a sharp dialectal-authenticity gap between entity- and context-level rewriting (DA 0.92 vs. 0.51). Despite lower register fidelity, context augmentation with curriculum training delivers the most consistent gains (Curras F1 +5.70 pp); entity augmentation lifts Lebanese F1 from a zero baseline to 50.00 on Lebanese-only training, a figure the 85-sentence test set makes coarse. Ablation, weight-sensitivity, threshold sweep, a random-selection control, and a second LLM backbone show that the dialectal-authenticity dimension carries most of Q(s)’s protective effect on Lebanese and that generator choice is itself a first-class register-preservation lever.

paper.title: Robustness of Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models to CheckList-Style Perturbations

author.affiliation: Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: We compare diffusion-based and autoregressive language models under CheckList-style perturbations. We frame semantics-preserving perturbations as potentially containing an off-manifold component and hypothesise that diffusion denoising can reduce the resulting output change relative to autoregressive decoding. We evaluate eight instruction-tuned 7-9B models (three diffusion, five autoregressive) across sentiment, QQP, and SQuAD using behavioural pass rates and a perturbation coefficient that measures output change relative to input change. Results are task-dependent. Behaviourally, diffusion gains 18.2 and 11.0 points overall on QQP and SQuAD, while autoregressive models perform better on the sentiment and SQuAD invariance slices. On QQP, the all-model coefficient ratio does not favour diffusion (\hat{γ}_{AR}/\hat{α}_{Diff} \approx 0.91); excluding two autoregressive models with strong label-prior effects as a diagnostic sensitivity analysis yields 1.23 overall and 1.48 on invariance tests. Diffusion also performs worse on perturbations that should change the output. Thus, the observed stability differences are task-conditional, and because the empirical diffusion coefficients exceed one, the experiments do not directly validate the contraction assumption of our theoretical proposition. Data and code are available at: https://github.com/AarushRathore1729/dlm_ar_final.

paper.title: DTS: Discriminant Truthfulness Scoring for Gradient-Free Hallucination Detection

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay and University of Illinois, Chicago

paper.abstract: Large language models can hallucinate with the same fluent confidence they bring to correct answers, making reliable hallucination detection essential for trustworthy deployment. Existing detectors based on LLM hidden states often rely on cosine or linear readouts that ignore the anisotropic structure of the representation space. We introduce DTS (Discriminant Truthfulness Scoring), a lightweight, gradient-free detector that whitens hidden activations using within-class covariance and scores responses with a closed-form Fisher discriminant. Across Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on four QA datasets, DTS ranks first in five of eight settings and second in the remaining three. Whitening improves over cosine scoring by 7.8 AUROC points on average, identifying the readout as a major bottleneck. When truthful and hallucinated representations overlap, class-mean steering provides additional gains without learning a steering vector. DTS requires only a single forward pass and closed-form computation, making it substantially cheaper than sampling- and gradient-based alternatives, while also extending effectively to long-form generation.

paper.title: Reset Is Not Recovery: Evaluating Recoverability from False Conversational Context via Sycophancy Hysteresis
paper.abstract: Grounded language models are usually evaluated by adding relevant context, but multi-turn dialogue also contains unsupported user claims that may contaminate later factual answers. We study post-pressure recoverability: whether a model returns to clean-context behavior after a user repeatedly advocates a wrong answer and then withdraws that pressure. We introduce a recovery-after-pressure protocol for multiple-choice factual dialogue and measure sycophancy hysteresis, the residual probability assigned to the user-advocated wrong answer relative to a clean-context counterfactual. Across seven instruction-tuned open-weight models and two factual benchmarks, ordinary reset often reduces but does not erase pressure-induced bias. History-preserving repairs such as user retraction, system reset, and self-verification recover only 2–3/14 model–dataset pairs under the strict clean-restoration diagnostic, whereas operations that change the effective context are substantially more reliable; the two conditions that remove the pressure-bearing history entirely, fresh-context deletion and context truncation, recover 14/14. In an oracle trusted-evidence condition across fourteen model–dataset pairs, preserving the pressure-bearing history while adding benchmark-derived trusted evidence increases accuracy from 0.368 to 0.929, while wrong-answer following falls from 41.2% to 4.3%. Controls show that the effect is not explained by dialogue length, repeated confidence, plausible distractors, mere false-answer mention, or option-label inertia. These results suggest that faithful grounded dialogue requires evaluating which prior context should be treated as evidence and which should be removed or quarantined before answering.
