paper.title: Groundedness Is Not Truth: Evidence-Chain Forensics for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: A single faithfulness score can hide failures that require different repairs: a RAG answer may be grounded in text whose source is stale, incomplete, contradicted, low-authority, or insufficient. We introduce ContextTrace, a deterministic, local-first SDK and CLI for evidence-chain forensics that separates claim support, citation state, source condition, abstention need, root cause, repair, and regression prevention. We also introduce Groundedness-Truth-Gap, a suite for controlled conformance, while frozen RAGTruth and stress tests serve as failure-safety controls. ContextTrace’s central contribution is an inspectable evidence-chain contract. On a fresh 84-case public-document evaluation, it catches 76 of 77 failure-bearing cases and preserves all seven clean cases (balanced accuracy 0.994; MCC 0.929), the same binary confusion counts as a frozen GPT-4.1-mini judge, while producing typed diagnostic records without additional model calls. The clean-case sample is small, and fine-grained label, root, and unverifiable attribution remains limited. Post-review counterfactuals further show strong dependence on source metadata and temporal cues. We release a blinded 50-case annotation packet and scorer; independent adjudication remains pending. Our claim is reproducible fail-closed diagnosis, not truth verification or broad evaluator superiority.

paper.title: Human-Perception-Aware but Not Yet Physically Grounded: Strengths and Failure Modes of Frontier Multimodal LLMs and the GroundVQA Benchmark
paper.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual question answering (VQA), OCR-intensive image understanding, and multimodal reasoning. However, they can still produce linguistically plausible answers that are not supported by visual evidence, particularly under ambiguous OCR, weak visual evidence, and challenging spatial or physical reasoning. We introduce GroundVQA, an adversarial VQA benchmark designed to evaluate visual grounding, hallucination resistance, OCR robustness, uncertainty handling, and spatial and physical reasoning. GroundVQA contains 3,877 manually reviewed question–answer pairs constructed from approximately 2,400 public-source images and around 100 self-collected real-world images. We evaluate representative frontier MLLMs on a stratified subset of GroundVQA and complement the quantitative evaluation with qualitative analyses of recurring model strengths and failure modes. Our findings highlight a persistent reliance on semantic priors when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, motivating evaluation frameworks that emphasize grounded reasoning, calibrated uncertainty, and adversarial premise rejection beyond conventional VQA accuracy.

paper.title: Polite on the Surface, Broken in Practice: A Curated Dataset for Fixing Generation and Register Failures in Low-Resource Bangla Text Generation
paper.abstract: Recent advances in Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) have improved cross-lingual conversational capabilities, yet generating reliable, institutionally usable text in low-resource languages like Bangla remains a critical bottleneck, particularly for compact, low-resource LLMs. Beyond surface fluency, state-of-the-art and small open-weight models frequently exhibit deeper generation failures in Bangla: incoherent or off-topic output, structural misformatting, and inconsistent honorific registers, that render text unusable in formal contexts. To address this, we introduce BLADE (BangLa Application and DialoguE generation), a culturally aligned instruction-tuning dataset and benchmarking framework comprising 4,196 curated interaction pairs. We use this resource to fine-tune and evaluate compact open-weight architectures, including DeepSeek-8B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, Qwen2, and TigerLLM-1B, via LoRA adapters under 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization on limited hardware. Our evaluations show that targeted fine-tuning on BLADE yields substantial improvements in generation reliability, structural fidelity, and register consistency even for the smallest models, establishing a rigorous benchmark for closing generation and pragmatic gaps in low-resource multilingual text generation. Code and dataset: https://github.com/ashuvo25/Bangla_Application_LLM

paper.title: Retrieve, Locate, Generate: An Oracle-Substitution Diagnostic for Literature-Grounded QA
paper.abstract: Literature-grounded question answering requires a system to retrieve the right paper, locate the right evidence within it, and generate an answer faithful to that evidence. These are three separate stages, each with its own failure mode. We present a stage-wise diagnostic study of this pipeline on LitTraceQA, a shared task requiring paper retrieval, coarse evidence localization (table/figure/page), and structured answer generation. Our pipeline combines cross-model hypothesis diversity for retrieval, a filter-then-rank evidence localizer (caption-pattern match, embedding similarity, evidence-type gate), and cross-model semantic entropy for generation-time answer aggregation and confidence estimation. We use an oracle-substitution ablation ladder, sequentially handing the pipeline the gold paper and then the gold evidence value, and reading off the resulting change in each stage’s own metric. These are sequential oracle-intervention gains, not an additive error decomposition: the stages are measured with different quantities and are not independent. Read that way, the ladder points at evidence localization as the dominant remediable bottleneck — multiple-choice accuracy rises from 0.42 with predicted evidence to 0.76 with the gold evidence value, and end-to-end accuracy stays near 0.29 even on the questions where retrieval already returned every gold paper. We also test whether cheap uncertainty signals computed at retrieval time predict which stage will fail before it does. Along the way we surface two infrastructure-level findings with direct implications for anyone building literature-grounded QA systems. First, evidence page numbers in this and similar benchmarks are keyed to a paper’s canonical published version rather than its arXiv preprint; a real failure mode when a paper has been substantively revised, though a systematic paired ablation across 45 questions finds it is an occasional rather than pervasive hazard in this pool. Second, a substantial fraction of papers hosted on OpenReview (ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS) are unreachable by ordinary scripted HTTP requests due to a JS bot-challenge, a venue-correlated failure mode unrelated to any modeling choice. We report our diagnostic protocol, quantitative results with bootstrap confidence intervals given the benchmark’s small public dev set, and a qualitative failure taxonomy, framing this as a resource and lessons-learned contribution rather than a leaderboard claim. All multiple-choice numbers are a best-case diagnostic condition: they assume access to the gold option text, which a genuine blind submission would not have.

paper.title: CITECHECK: Retrieval-Grounded Detection of LLM Citation Hallucinations in Scientific Text
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate scientific reports, but they can produce references that appear plausible while containing corrupted metadata or pointing to papers that do not exist. We introduce CITECHECK, a hybrid framework for citation hallucination detection that verifies whether a citation corresponds to a real scholarly work and whether its metadata is faithful to that work. CITECHECK retrieves candidate publications from external scholarly sources, compares the citation against the retrieved candidate using a structured LLM verifier, and maps verifier scores into three labels: Exact, Minor, and Major. We also construct a 982-citation physics benchmark with controlled corruptions that capture both subtle metadata drift and fully fabricated references. On the held-out test set, CITECHECK achieves 88.7 macro-F1 and 88.9% accuracy, outperforming GPT, Claude, and Gemini baselines, including web-search and few-shot variants. These results show that reliable citation verification benefits from combining scholarly retrieval, structured LLM-based comparison, and calibrated decision rules.

paper.title: GRACE: Generating Conflict-Aware Cases for Evaluating Policy Compliance in Enterprise Conversational AI
paper.abstract: Policy compliance in enterprise conversational AI is not binary: the same response can satisfy one stakeholder’s policy while violating another’s. Existing evaluations largely treat compliance as a single-policy problem, which makes cross-role conflict cases difficult to construct and assess. GRACE (Generating Conflict-Aware Cases for Evaluating Policy Compliance) addresses this gap by generating matched normal and conflict cases from the same underlying scenario, assigning role-wise expected verdicts through independent per-role policy evaluation, and scoring responses independently for each role rather than collapsing compliance into a single binary label. Across four domains, this process yields 1,109 labeled scenarios, including 309 cross-role conflicts. Evaluating five LLMs shows that deny cases are easiest, allow cases are depressed by over-refusal, and conflict cases are consistently hardest, revealing failures that single-label evaluation obscures. Per-persona analysis further shows that these errors are localized to specific domain-role combinations rather than uniform across models. GRACE therefore supports both policy review and deployment-time model selection.

paper.title: StreamSense: A Content- and Resource-Aware Edge Agent for Adaptive Bitrate Streaming

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) decision-making is essential for optimizing Quality of Experience (QoE) in video streaming. Traditional ABR methods typically lack fine-grained content understanding and face challenges in balancing multi-dimensional QoE objectives under real-world edge device constraints. To overcome these limitations, we propose **StreamSense Agent**, a novel framework that reformulates ABR as a sequential decision-making process informed by content and network awareness. Our approach introduces three key innovations: (1) a Dynamic Content-Aware Entity Graph (D-CAEG) for structured video representation, (2) a composite QoE-driven optimization objective integrating perceptual quality, rebuffering, smoothness, and computational cost, and (3) a hierarchical resource-aware architecture enabling real-time control through an efficient lightweight actor. We further adopt an offline-to-online co-adaptation training paradigm with federated learning for continuous adaptation. Since effective ABR control requires the same core competencies as general sequential decision-making—multi-step planning across future video chunks, dynamic information gathering from heterogeneous network signals, and adaptive strategy adjustment under resource constraints—we validate these transferable capabilities on five established benchmarks. Specifically, multi-hop search tasks (BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH) mirror the integration of dispersed network-trace and content-complexity signals into a bitrate plan; complex navigation tasks (WebWalkerQA) correspond to sequential buffer-state traversal under volatile bandwidth; and information-extraction tasks (Xbench-DS, SimpleQA) reflect the precision required when reading real-time streaming telemetry. StreamSense Agent achieves state-of-the-art results, attaining accuracy of 16.7% on BrowseComp, 30.5% on BrowseComp-ZH, 42.1% on Xbench-DS, and 54.2% on WebWalkerQA. Deployment-oriented evaluations further confirm its computational efficiency, achieving an inference throughput of 12.5 requests per second with a memory footprint of only 2,100 MB under edge-like constraints, yielding a normalized QoE score of 0.92. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the necessity of each proposed component. This work establishes a new paradigm for intelligent, edge-deployable bitrate adaptation.

paper.title: From Position Bias to Position-Stable Agreement: Testing What LLM Judges Evaluate
paper.abstract: Pairwise LLM-as-judge evaluation should preserve response identity when presentation order changes. Across four judge models, short A/B prompts yield 70–100% second-position selection (72/80 comparisons overall). Targeted prompt ablations show format sensitivity: label changes alter parsed choices, and a neutral buffer produces complete first-position selection on 59 fixed-order comparisons, reversing rather than removing position preference. We use a position-swapped evaluation protocol, retaining a directional verdict only when both orders select the same response. In a new 16-condition GPT-4.1 factorial audit, analysis-first and a verdict prefix raise directional coverage by 5.6 and 6.5 percentage points, respectively. On 40 Arena-Hard queries with three generators, the 120 pairs comprise 62 directional results, no double ties, 14 swap failures, and 44 invalid pairs. Cross-Model Agreement (CMA) yields 25 unique query winners. A retrospective domain-routing check predicts 17 of these 25 labels using rules fitted outside each test fold. These labels and any oracle score remain judge-relative; human-preference validity and downstream training gains are not established.

paper.title: Preserving Evidence Anchors: Query-Rewriting Guardrails for Retrieval-Side Grounding
paper.abstract: Query rewriting is now a common preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, yet it can silently damage grounding before generation begins: a fluent rewrite may drop the exact terms that retrieve the evidence. We study this retrieval-interface failure mode across five benchmarks, three retriever families, three rewriting strategies, and two open-weight LLMs. In the main Zephyr-7B setting, unconstrained rewriting degrades nDCG@10 by more than 0.05 for 26–76% of queries, with harmful cases often exhibiting evidence-anchor drift: rare domain terms, named entities, and numerics are replaced by less discriminative paraphrases. We propose a training-free constraint layer that identifies candidate evidence anchors, prompts the LLM to preserve them, verifies preservation deterministically, and falls back to the original query when verification fails. The method requires no retriever training, no logit access, and no constrained decoder. It reduces mean qrel-observed harm from 48% to 10% on BEIR and from 26% to 6% on Natural Questions, with the same qualitative pattern across tested retrievers, rewriting strategies, and 7B open-weight models. We isolate benchmark-labeled evidence exposure as a pre-generation condition for downstream attribution rather than evaluating generated answers. The results support a practical design principle: LLMs may expand retrieval queries, but the retrieval interface should explicitly protect the lexical anchors on which evidence access depends.

paper.title: Grounding Creative Query Suggestions, Faithfully and Efficiently: From Corpus-Grounded Supervision to Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Creative search platforms help users turn short, vague queries into searches and generation prompts. To be useful, a suggestion has to fit the context it appears in, the asset type, the season, and the user’s region, and it has to be grounded in assets the platform can actually retrieve. A fluent suggestion that returns nothing wastes the user’s attention and erodes trust. Building such a system is hard because there is no ready-made training data: user logs are sparse, noisy, and privacy-constrained, and they say nothing about context or grounding. We first solve this with corpus-grounded synthetic supervision. A two-stage offline pipeline turns 59M asset captions into context-aware training data, constrained by a Creative Knowledge Graph and grounded through retrieval, and fine-tunes a single low-latency model that serves related suggestions, refinements, and generation-ready prompts in one retrieval-free step. We check grounding by running suggestions against the production index: offline, retrieval grounding raises the share of well-grounded suggestions by over 30% relative, and in production about 99% of served suggestions return real assets (a null rate near 1%). The deployed system is preferred over the prior log-based suggester in human evaluation and improved the primary business metric in production. As the system reached new surfaces, two requirements emerged that the supervised data met poorly: single-word suggestions for space-constrained interfaces, and selective seasonal and regional context—added in the harder cases the deployed model missed, and suppressed where it does not apply. Rather than regenerate the data and retrain, we add a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) stage whose hybrid reward pairs an LLM judge with programmatic checks for format, length, and diversity. It improves seasonal alignment by 18.6 and regional alignment by 5.2 points (on a 0 to 100 judge scale) and raises single-word compliance from 15.1% to 99.1%, a format absent from the supervised data, while keeping relevance and diversity intact and leaving the retrieval-free serving path unchanged.

paper.title: The Coin Flip Judge? Reliability and Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge is widely used to rank model outputs and populate leaderboards, yet its run-to-run reliability is under-characterized. We study repeated identical evaluations across six judges from three providers spanning three model generations (2024-2026), with 50 pairwise and 50 pointwise trials per question on 29 tasks. Three findings stand out. First, pairwise verdicts are unstable, with an 11-14% mean flip rate on identical re-runs, and this has not improved across generations: the newest, cheapest deployable judges flip just as often as 2024 models. Second, a dedicated swap-order experiment (8,700 judgments) shows the fixed-order asymmetry is order bias, not self-preference, and that order bias has not been fixed either: the 2026 judges reverse its direction, favouring the second slot where earlier judges favoured the first, so a first-position check records them as unbiased while they still decide 21-41% of matched comparisons on slot rather than content. Third, forced-choice verdicts and scalar scores come apart, and ~11 repeated trials are needed to stabilize a verdict. We argue that multi-trial aggregation, symmetric order randomization, and uncertainty reporting should be standard practice.

paper.title: The Attribution–Compression Frontier in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: Context compression reduces generator input in retrieval-augmented generation, but answer quality alone does not characterize citation attribution. We measure citation attribution across compression methods and budgets, comparing reranking, extractive selection, abstractive summarization, token pruning, and an extract-cluster-rewrite construction on ASQA and QASPER under a fixed generator and primary entailment evaluator. On ASQA at a nominal 0.25 budget (achieved compression 0.08), a RECOMP-style compressor’s citations score 0.86 precision against its summaries but 0.12 against source spans under our re-attributability protocol. These estimates depend on a shared NLI model for span recovery and citation scoring and lack independent human calibration. Extractive selection’s observed grounded precision ranges from 0.43 to 0.49 across nominal budgets from one-half to one-tenth of the ASQA context, while answer quality declines. For the same RECOMP setting, claim verification after source recovery yields an unsupported rate of 0.88 versus 0.17 when checking summaries. This gap persists beyond structural rejection of missing provenance, but remains evaluator-dependent. A 200-question TRUE T5-XXL audit also finds emitted–grounded gaps under both fixed and recomputed source mappings, without establishing human-calibrated support rates.

paper.title: Budget-Aware Compression Pipeline for Single-GPU LLM Inference: Methods, Trade-offs, and Coupling Effects
paper.abstract: Single-GPU deployment of 70B-parameter language models on an NVIDIA GPU is constrained by device memory, long-context throughput, and engineering integration cost. We cast single-GPU inference as a budget-aware design problem over these three axes and study how pruning, quantization, and KV-cache compression interact under realistic execution. Controlled ablations show that layer-wise pruning makes weight quantization more robust. KV-cache sparsification complements INT8 KV quantization by reducing memory without hurting decoding speed, while static vector quantizers often conflict with dynamic caching. Guided by these coupling results and explicit budget tracking, we assembled a practical pipeline and compressed a 70B model to about 33 GB, sustained about 57 tokens/s on 10k token prompts on a single A40, and kept absolute accuracy within 5% on common and reasoning benchmarks. We contribute design rules and a reproducible evaluation protocol that jointly report quality, memory, and end-to-end speed, and we provide a foundation for automated pipeline search under realistic single-GPU constraints.

paper.title: Leveraging Low-Level Symbolic Competences for Unsupervised Grounding in Hallucination Detection
paper.abstract: Hallucination—where a language model generates outputs that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the source—is a major challenge for both prompted and fine-tuned language models. Detecting hallucinations is difficult due to the opaque reasoning processes of LLMs, which often provide little insight into why a model’s output may be inaccurate.In this work, we investigate whether an LLM can use an alternative, low level, symbolic competence such as SQL for unsupervised hallucination detection in some high level task. For this, we make an LLM build an SQL database from reference documents. This SQL database is then used for reasoning over the reference and the sampled response in a hallucination detection pipeline that is grounded in the database, thereby providing a neurosymbolic checkup.On RAGTruth and DiaHalu hallucination detection datasets, we find that our approach improves on direct prediction and competes with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods, while not requiring domain-specific fine-tuning. Instead it relies on a low-level general competence already present in LLMs. This warrants further investigation of low-level LLM competences in neurosymbolic approaches.

paper.title: The Coverage Illusion: From Pre-retrieval Routing Failure to Post-retrieval Cascades in a Production RAG System
paper.abstract: In modern RAG pipelines, query augmentation methods such as HyDE and query expansion are applied to every query, resulting in substantial LLM inference costs and increased end-to-end latency. The empirical justification for this overhead in real production traffic remains largely unexplored. We present a case study of the Danish National Encyclopedia, evaluating five retrieval workflows over 20,000 query–workflow pairs from production traffic and synthetic conditions. In this system, synthetic queries suggest that LLM augmentation is needed for over 90% of queries to achieve high retrieval coverage. However, under our production deferral policy, only 27.8% of real user queries need LLM augmentation. We call this gap the Coverage Illusion and attribute it to a structural mismatch between synthetic and real query distributions. Pre-retrieval routing cannot resolve this gap, as the need for LLM augmentation is only revealed after searching the index, a result confirmed by our evaluation of four machine learning paradigms. The coverage gap, undetectable from the query alone, motivates a post-retrieval cascade that runs workflows in cheapest-first order and escalates to LLM augmentation only when a step returns no documents. Operating entirely without training overhead or secondary serving infrastructure, the cascade improves quality by +0.140 Composite Overall points over Always-HyDE, reduces latency by 31.8%, and serves 72.2% of real user queries without LLM augmentation.

paper.title: When Models Defer to Wrong Answers: A Robustness Audit of Source-Attributed Cues in Multiple-Choice QA
paper.abstract: Language models often receive a question together with a claim about what another source answered. We audit whether such claims destabilize answers in multiple-choice question answering. For each item, we hold one wrong option fixed across misleading conditions and vary the cue template attached to it. We introduce neutral-conditioned misleading cue adoption rate (NC-MCAR), which measures switches to that option only on valid cued trials where the same model first selected the gold answer under a neutral prompt. This is a measure of answer instability, not proof that the model knew the answer or that all deference is irrational. We evaluate four instruction-following models on MMLU-Pro and IndicMMLU-Pro in English, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, and Telugu. Across 220,000 outputs, the expert template yields 41.1% aggregate NC-MCAR, compared with 12.5% for the majority template. These two conditions use the same wrong option and final instruction. Filler accuracy remains well above expert-wrong accuracy, while correct-cue prompts have high valid-response accuracy. The audit documents answer instability relevant to grounding under the tested forced-choice prompts: a bare, unverified source claim can outweigh an answer that was previously consistent with the task evidence.

paper.title: Does the Selected Object Reach the Reader? Auditing Identity Handoffs in Grounded Language-Model Pipelines

author.affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Grounded language-model pipelines can be divided into three stages: selecting an object, retrieving passages for it, and using that evidence to answer. If the selected object must reach the reader, losing it breaks the handoff. Benchmark recall checks the dataset-linked object, which can differ. We audit 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. On 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage, exact key lookup and exact title matching return the object every time. With every ranked rule given the same decoded selected title, body-only BM25 omits it on 389 records (26.6%) at cutoff five, while hybrid retrieval with reranking omits it on 14 (1.0%). The two identities differ on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, their top-five checks disagree on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen reader comparisons associate the aligned object’s presence with 28.6 to 31.0 points higher exact match. In a deliberately selected 64-item cohort, removing that passage sharply lowers exact match, while removing a similar-length comparison passage does not reproduce the drop. We release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP), an executable record of the target, returned-ID field, cutoff, membership rule, and complete expected population, with data and an offline replay.

paper.title: Learning from Dialogue Traces: Retrieval-Guided Tool Use and Response Generation for Task-Oriented Dialogue Agents

author.affiliation: AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Effective task-oriented dialogue (TOD) requires agents to coordinate two tightly coupled decisions of when to invoke external tools and how to formulate a response that satisfies the user’s goal. However, their turn-level behavior remains weakly grounded under fixed zero-shot prompts. Meanwhile, existing retrieval-based TOD agents primarily retrieve task-relevant content from external knowledge sources, guiding which information to include but offering limited guidance on how to select tools and formulate responses in similar dialogue contexts. To mitigate this, we introduce TRACE, a Turn-level Retrieval Agent with Contextual Experiences for TOD [<https://github.com/aistairc/TRACE-TOD>]. Instead of relying on retrieved factual records alone, TRACE retrieves goal-conditioned dialogue snippets as behavioral demonstrations at each turn. These snippets capture similar user goals, constraints, tool-use decisions, and response patterns to guide both tool calls and response generation. Experiments on MultiWOZ 2.1 and Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD) show that TRACE improves Inform and Success over a competitive LLM agent and end-to-end fine-tuned models under both simulation-based and static-user evaluations. Human evaluation and retrieval-focused analyses further show that goal-conditioned snippets and retrieval quality drive these gains.

paper.title: Enhancing Small Language Models in RAG via Triplet-Guided In-Context Distillation

author.affiliation: AICORN Project and Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used for knowledge-intensive question answering (QA) but typically relies on large language models (LLMs) as generators, which raises cost and privacy concerns. We propose TripletRAG, a simple, training-free method that converts LLM-teacher behavior into triplets (synthetic question, retrieved passages, reference answer), which are then provided as exemplar context to a small language model (SLM) at inference. TripletRAG requires only offline synthetic QA generation and retrieval; no SLM finetuning is needed. Across SQuAD and Natural Questions (KILT) datasets, triplet guidance substantially increases judge-based accuracy, and improves groundedness on SQuAD for models in the 1B–3B parameter range, with negligible or inconsistent gains for larger models (7B+). Compared to a strong lightweight baseline (MiniRAG), TripletRAG gives markedly better groundedness and correctness while keeping the pipeline simple and practical.

paper.title: Why Your Deep Research Agent Fails? On Hallucination Evaluation in Full Research Trajectory
paper.abstract: Diagnosing failure patterns in Deep Research Agents (DRAs) remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks predominantly rely on end-to-end evaluation, obscuring intermediate hallucinations that accumulate throughout the research trajectory. To bridge this gap, we propose a shift from outcome-based to **process-aware evaluation** by auditing hallucinations in the full *plan-search-summarize* trajectory. We introduce the **PING Taxonomy**, which categorizes DRA hallucinations into four complementary types: **P**ropagation, **I**ntent, **N**oise-induced, and **G**rounding. We further instantiate this taxonomy into a fine-grained evaluation framework that decomposes trajectories into atomic actions, claims, and sub-queries for rigorous verification, and we validate its reliability on standard fact-checking benchmarks and human-reviewed trajectories. Leveraging this framework to isolate 100 hallucination-prone tasks, including adversarial scenarios, we curate **DeepHalluBench**. Experiments on six representative DRAs show that, on our hallucination-prone stress-test set, all evaluated systems still exhibit non-negligible reliability gaps. Furthermore, our diagnostic analysis traces these failures to systemic deficits, especially hallucination propagation and cognitive biases, providing actionable insights for future architectural optimization. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhao-zhan/DeepHalluBench.

paper.title: A Modular Approach to Conversational Object Grounding in 3D Scenes Using VLMs and Prompt Chaining

author.affiliation: University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge

paper.abstract: We introduce Conversational Object Grounding, a new task in which an agent must identify a target object in a complex 3D scene by engaging in natural language dialogue with a user who knows the target. It extends multimodal reference resolution on a single referring expression to conversations over multiple turns, combining it with clarification question generation and answer understanding to resolve ambiguities. For this task, we propose a zero-shot modular approach that combines the reference resolution, object captioning, and dialogue capabilities of foundation models, using prompt chaining in conjunction with an image-grounded scene graph. Evaluations on a new benchmark constructed with 3D scenes from ScanNet show that the proposed modular approach outperforms end-to-end baselines in terms of both grounding performance (up to 13% improvement) and image processing cost (up to 63% reduction).

paper.title: BAND: Bias-Aware Retrieval Debiasing for Demographic Robustness in Retrieval-Augmented Medical Question Answering
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly adopted in medical question answering, where generated answers depend heavily on retrieved biomedical evidence. However, demographic perturbations in clinical queries can substantially alter retrieval behavior, causing retrievers to surface demographically correlated yet clinically irrelevant evidence. We refer to this phenomenon as retrieval shift, where demographic-sensitive retrieval representations propagate bias into downstream generation. To investigate this issue, we construct a demographically perturbed MedQA dataset and systematically analyze retrieval instability under demographic perturbations across representative medical RAG systems. Our analysis shows that RAG systems are substantially more sensitive to demographic perturbations than standalone LLMs, indicating that retrieval plays a central role in propagating demographic bias. To mitigate retrieval shift, we propose Bias-Aware Neutral Debiasing (BAND), a rotation-based retrieval debiasing framework that suppresses demographic-sensitive retrieval directions while maintaining clinically relevant retrieval behavior. Experiments demonstrate that our method consistently reduces retrieval shift while largely preserving downstream task performance across multiple medical RAG systems. Our code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/hrimlee/BAND

paper.title: Agents Out of Bounds: A Taxonomy of Architectural Drift and a Deployment-Ready Guardrail Framework for LLM Coding Agents
paper.abstract: LLM coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code now author a large share of the code that teams merge, and they are active in an estimated 22% of public GitHub projects. The output is fast and usually correct in the small. The trouble is that an agent optimizes for the task in front of it, not the global shape of the system. That cost is now measurable. Agent adoption causally raises code complexity by about 42% and static-analysis warnings by about 30%, and the most common reason an agent’s patch fails is a shallow grasp of the surrounding architecture. We call this widening gap between a system’s intended and realized architecture architectural drift. The obvious remedy, stating the rules in the prompt, does not hold at repository scale; the evidence is that only deterministic, executable enforcement conforms reliably. We make two contributions. The first is a taxonomy of LLM-induced architectural drift: five deterministically enforceable families plus one open frontier, each tied to the architectural primitive it corrupts and the model behavior that produces it. The second is GyroCompass, a deployment-oriented framework. It extracts a living architecture model from source, serves that model to the agent as planning-time context (prevention), and enforces it through a deterministic gate that, run in CI, cannot be bypassed (detection). On a labeled benchmark of 208 cases (104 violations, 104 realistic decoys) spanning Python and JavaScript/TypeScript, GyroCompass reaches 88.5% recall at a 5.8% false-positive rate, versus 57.7% recall at 42.3% false positives for a naive pattern baseline (McNemar p<0.001); on the original 54-case core it separates violations from look-alikes at 100% recall and zero false positives. Head-to-head on matched subsets, a five-tool comparison (Semgrep, Bandit, CodeQL, pip-audit, import-linter) reaches at most 65% recall. Extraction runs at over 800 files per second, cheap enough to apply on every commit, and its output matches independently constructed references at 0.95-1.0 component precision/recall across four repositories. In an added-line analysis of 1,779 commits of a 10k-star production repository whose maintainers document their layering rules for AI agents, violations of the documented intent continued to land, including after an agent-facing AGENTS.md stated the rules,which is the enforcement gap GyroCompass closes. On the prevention side, serving the architecture to a coding agent as context shifts its layering behavior, but the effect is model-dependent across three model families, which is itself why the deterministic gate, not prompt context, is the binding guarantee. We discuss the prevention/detection trade-off, lessons from instrumenting agent workflows, and what reliable guardrails ask of a team in practice. GyroCompass is a working system intended for real-world deployment; benchmark, harness, and analysis scripts are released.

paper.title: When Targeted Grounded Gains Hide Complementary Abstraction Regression: DION-Bench and a Conjunctive Evaluation Protocol
paper.abstract: Post-training with internal feedback can improve a targeted knowledge-grounded behavior while silently degrading complementary abstraction and logical-consistency capabilities. We propose a conjunctive evaluation protocol that accepts a method only when a designated target improves and complementary probes remain non-inferior (with a stricter secondary criterion requiring complementary equivalence), while also reporting retention and predictive drift. We instantiate the protocol in DION-Bench, combining two lexical/ontological probes (same-category exceptions; abstraction recovery) with a synthetic SAT-checked logical-consistency probe. On Qwen3-8B-Base, a task-specific self-judged DPO adaptation improves OntoNeg-WN by 5.27 percentage points but reduces ConceptShift by 37.50 points—despite humans reaching 82.7% and frontier LLMs 44–73% on OntoNeg—whereas mean change across five external accuracy suites is only −1.70 points. A development-tuned decoding rule partially mitigates ConceptShift regression to 12.93/14.60 points on the original/holdout splits while retaining most of the target gain. These results show that faithful post-training claims require joint reporting of gain, complementary abstraction regression, retention, drift, and equivalence—not proof that a single shared knowledge item degraded.

paper.title: Evidence-Indexed Slide Narration With Heuristic Checks and Template Fallback

author.affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder and ebay Inc.

paper.abstract: Slide narration generation can introduce unsupported visual or decorative claims. We describe a pipeline that indexes slide content with deterministic identifiers, generates an internally cited template, and applies heuristic checks before and after an optional language-model rewrite. A narration-stage study covers 30 publicly sourced presentations (279 slides). The same decks and procedure were used, but stochastic vision evidence was regenerated by condition. In one run per condition, the complete configuration produced 5/279 proxy flags (1.79%) versus 22/279 (7.89%) for A1, a 77.3% relative difference (slide-paired exact p ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻⁴; deck-blocked p = 0.0156); B produced 20/279 (7.17%). Saved labels mark 225/279 condition-C outputs as template fallbacks. Post-rewrite verdicts were not saved, and six outputs retained model narration when no nonempty verified template was available. The proxy has F1 = 0.60 against judgments based on extracted context rather than rendered slides. These are observed system-level proxy rates, not component attribution or evidence that hallucination is eliminated.

paper.title: Default Zero-Shot LLM APIs Over-Flag Indian Financial SMS: A Policy-Aligned Benchmark and Template-Level Pre-Deployment Audit

author.affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder and ebay Inc.

paper.abstract: Generic ham/spam labels do not define a financial-fraud blocking policy. We present a 1,393-message policy-aligned Indian SMS benchmark in Hindi, Hinglish, and English-India, separating source labels, fraud/non-fraud/unclear adjudication, and allow/review/block actions. GPT-4o and Gemini helped adjudicate source-positive messages, so positive metrics are secondary. Our primary endpoint is false-positive rate (FPR) on 1,294 policy-negatives: 1,222 untouched source negatives plus 72 source positives converted to safe. Under a common minimal prompt, six LLM APIs exceed illustrative 1% FPR gates on Bank and UPI templates. GPT-4o-mini records 77.3% and 56.9% FPR; a fine-tuned 270M XLM-R records 0.0% on both, 0.4% globally, and 0.980 recall. Policy definitions and seven examples reduce GPT-4o to 0.0% Bank/UPI and 1.5% global FPR at 0.949 recall; Claude reaches 1.8% at 0.960 recall. Prompting changes which gate fails. GPT-4o P3 and the AND consensus meet the FPR gates at lower policy-label recall; the local model meets both FPR and recall gates on this benchmark. Because positive labels partly use GPT-4o/Gemini, recall and F1 are secondary, not an overall ranking. We release labels, prompts, parsed decisions, analysis code, and checkpoints without a production or unseen-institution claim.

paper.title: PageRecall: Measuring Page Selection in Literature-Grounded Question Answering
paper.abstract: We describe our system for LitTraceQA (GroundLM @ EMNLP 2026): given a research question, retrieve the relevant papers from a pool of 27,487, cite the page and the table or figure where the answer lives, and answer in a requested format. Our main finding is that evidence grounding is limited by retrieval, not by reading. The page selector put the annotator’s page, which we call the gold page, in front of the model that locates evidence only about half the time (52.6% gold-page recall), while that model, given the page, cited the right one in 45 of the 48 locators it emitted (94%). When the page was missing it rarely said so: of 45 such cases it returned nothing 14 times, a wrong page 24 times, and a correct page 7 times, so the pipeline failed quietly almost twice as often as it failed visibly. Since the failure was that the right page was never shown, the fix is to stop choosing: each retrieved paper fits in the model’s context, so we show it whole. Page ranking survives only as a fallback inside papers too long to fit, which no test-split paper was, and gold-page recall reaches 100% on the papers we can parse. Separately, questions that identify their target by position rather than content, such as "the first author of the 24th reference", are served by parsing rather than retrieval: we resolve the bibliography into an addressable list, which also supplies identifiers the evidence metric scores. The final system scores 0.762 paper F_1, 0.441 evidence F_1 and 0.920 multiple-choice accuracy on the held-out test split. Because the pipeline depends on a closed model without seed control, we release a harness that verifies the paper’s central claims against committed artifacts.

paper.title: LitTraceQA: A Benchmark for Multi-Stage Grounding and Verification in Scientific Question Answering
paper.abstract: Scientific question answering is useful only when readers can recover the papers and evidence behind an answer. Yet many benchmarks either provide the source document or score only the final response, obscuring failures in literature retrieval and evidence localization. We present LitTraceQA, a literature-grounded question answering benchmark in which a system must return a connected trace: canonical paper identifiers, typed evidence locations, and a checkable answer. The collection contains 4,978 unique questions grounded in 4,859 papers and covers tables, figures, text spans, equations or algorithms, and citation contexts. Of these questions, 64.85% require multiple papers; answers use multiple-choice or structured-table formats; and 61.9% are missed by every memory-only challenger used during construction. We describe a generate-and-ground-challenge pipeline and an evaluation protocol that reports paper retrieval, evidence grounding, answer correctness, and strict joint success separately. LitTraceQA therefore tests whether scientific QA systems can produce answers whose provenance is inspectable, rather than merely plausible.

paper.title: CoVeR-VQA: Multi-Stage Evidence Verification for GoldenViewVQA
paper.abstract: GoldenViewVQA requires models to jointly answer driving-scene questions and identify the camera view containing the supporting visual evidence, making precise evidence localization as important as answer correctness. We present **CoVeR-VQA**, a training-free multi-stage verification and correction framework for grounded multi-view VQA. Starting from GPT-5.6 zero-shot predictions, CoVeR-VQA progressively applies view-specific verification with Gemini-3.6-Flash, prior-guided joint verification with Claude-Opus-5, and cross-split group-level verification that exploits semantically filtered question groups from shared multi-view scenes and validation-derived prior knowledge. On the official GoldenViewVQA test set, the four-stage CoVeR-VQA pipeline achieves 84.75% Joint Accuracy, improving the GPT-5.6 zero-shot baseline by 13.56 percentage points, while reaching 94.92% Answer Accuracy and 86.44% View Accuracy. The final submitted run achieves 88.14% Joint Accuracy after two additional evaluator-informed post-hoc corrections. Our analysis shows that supporting-view localization remains the primary source of residual errors, highlighting the importance of explicit evidence verification for reliable multi-view multimodal reasoning.

paper.title: A Non-Visual Baseline for Multi-View Visual Question Answering on GoldenViewVQA
paper.abstract: We present a non-visual baseline for GoldenViewVQA, a benchmark for multi-view visual question answering with evidence-source identification. The baseline reaches a joint accuracy of 0.7119 on the hidden test split and uses no visual input. Its view prediction is the fixed label CAM_FRONT, which reaches 0.7797 view accuracy on the test split, while Qwen3-4B predicts the answer from the question, answer options, and non-visual metadata with 0.8475 answer accuracy. These results show that the current benchmark permits substantial performance without image access. We analyze the supporting-view prior and performance across question groups, and discuss benchmark changes that could reduce reliance on non-visual shortcuts. We present this run as a strong non-visual baseline, not as evidence that vision is unnecessary for driving question answering. Code: https://github.com/aravind-mandiga/groundlm-goldenviewvqa.

paper.title: Combining RAG and Agentic Research for Evidence-Grounded Scientific Question Answering
paper.abstract: We present ThousandOfWind’s hybrid system for GroundLM 2026 LitTraceQA, combining traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with code-agent research. Agents design question-specific search scripts, revise them as evidence emerges, and reconcile their findings with RAG candidates. The required-test configuration starts with independent research and accepts subsequent revisions through field-level confidence gates and table-structure checks. Using GPT-5.6 Terra in GitHub Copilot CLI, the system raises the 71-question test composite from 0.3567 to 0.7374 and multiple-choice accuracy from 18/50 to 50/50. Macro table cell accuracy reaches 0.2698, leaving structured assembly as the main bottleneck. Our analysis explains the limits of row-key-preserving repair and motivates source-supported structural editing.

paper.title: Maddies at GroundLM 2026 Shared Tasks: Answer-Preserving Visual Re-grounding for Multi-View Driving VQA
paper.abstract: GoldenViewVQA asks a multimodal model to answer a driving-scene question and identify the synchronized camera view that supports its answer. Our first system, QAVEL, used option blind routing, local image inspection, pairwise view selection, and a final verifier. Tests with GPT-5.6 Luna and Terra showed a recurring problem: extra stages often replaced correct direct predictions, and higher reasoning effort did not repair the cascade. We therefore built Joint Answer-preserving Visual Re-grounding (JAVR) around a GPT-5.6 Sol joint prediction. JAVR freezes the answer, aligns the queried actor or condition across all six views, revisits disputed cameras with target-specific crops, and changes only the view when a restricted comparator certifies an exact, direct, and complete evidence source. On the 55-item development set, JAVR produced a descriptive one item increase over its Sol anchor, from 46 to 47 jointly correct predictions, without changing any answer. Our official 59-item test submission reached 79.66% joint accuracy, 81.36% view accuracy, and 94.92% answer accuracy

paper.title: TRACE: Target-Aware Retrieval, Attributed Evidence, and Contract-Constrained Extraction for LitTraceQA

author.affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder and ebay Inc.

paper.abstract: Finding a relevant paper is not the same as producing a verifiable answer from it. LitTraceQA requires canonical paper identifiers, exact evidence at the page or object level, and typed answers that match the evaluator. We call the separation between source access and scorer-visible correctness the grounding contract gap. TRACE - Target-Aware Retrieval, Attributed Evidence, and Contract-Constrained Extraction - addresses this gap with target-grouped retrieval, independent typed evidence localization, multimodal table extraction, schema-driven table construction, and fail-closed validation. It indexes 27,487 papers through passage, object, alias, citation, and dense representations while retaining the question target behind each signal. For tables, TRACE predicts the observation unit before extracting values and assembles rows with evaluator-compatible key normalization. Our audited selected clean-track artifact scores 0.760613 on the official 71-question test set, including 0.9728 paper F1, 0.6847 evidence F1, 0.9800 multiple-choice accuracy, 0.5423 table-row F1, and 0.3508 macro cell accuracy. On 11 public-development table records, a clean baseline and coordinate-aware visual fill obtain row F1 of 0.291 and 0.411, respectively; this diagnostic comparison includes fallback outputs and is not an official-test claim. Remaining errors chiefly concern locator, observation-unit, row-key, and source-value identity.

paper.title: SAGE: Slot-Aware Grounded Evidence Acquisition for LitTraceQA

author.affiliation: Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University and Shanghai Jiaotong University

paper.abstract: Literature-grounded question answering requires a system to retrieve the right papers, locate answer-bearing content in heterogeneous PDFs, and return an answer whose evidence locators can be restored from the retrieved documents. We describe SAGE, an evidence-first system for LitTraceQA that separates these dependencies. A query-only evidence plan converts a question and its public answer contract into typed evidence obligations. The system retrieves candidate papers from official metadata, acquires and parses their PDFs into provenance-preserving text and object records, reranks record-aware text and image projections, and selects a bounded evidence package with explicit slots, modality, and cross-paper coverage priorities. A multimodal generator then answers with the fixed package, while deterministic normalization permits only candidate paper IDs and locators recoverable from selected parser records. Overall, SAGE adopts an evidence-first design that separates paper retrieval, fine-grained evidence acquisition, set-level selection, and grounded answer generation while preserving provenance throughout the pipeline. On the official evaluation, the system performs strongly in paper retrieval and multiple-choice answering, whereas fine-grained evidence grounding and structured table prediction remain more challenging.

paper.title: OdeD at GroundLM 2026 Shared Tasks: Reading the Scorer for Literature-Grounded QA
paper.abstract: We describe team OdeD’s submission to LitTraceQA, the literature-grounded question answering task at GroundLM 2026. The task scores three coupled outputs: paper identifiers, coarse evidence locators, and answers in multiple-choice or table form. Our best official score on the 71-question held-out test split is 0.7649, against 0.4563 for our first submission and 0.5519 for our best fully automated one. Little of that improvement came from the retrieval-and-reading pipeline we began with; most of it came from two other sources. Reading the released evaluator showed the metric to be more asymmetric than it appears: paper F1 and evidence F1 carry weight 1/3 each while each of the three answer metrics carries 1/9. The evidence key is also a coarse tuple, so a correct value on a correct page scores zero when the source type or the visible object id is wrong. The 55-example development split then served to recover the dataset’s annotation conventions rather than as a tuning set, and our own submission history became a measuring instrument. Each macro metric is a mean of a small number of rational per-question values, so a controlled change to one prediction file often admits a single arithmetic explanation. Two predicted deltas returned exact to four decimals. We report the conventions this recovered, six heuristics it refuted, four bugs it exposed in our own verifiers, and the limitation that much of our final score reflects per-question auditing and leaderboard feedback rather than a system that would generalise.

paper.title: Lit3R: Retrieve–Relate–Read for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering over Scientific Literature

author.affiliation: Tohoku University and DENTSU SOKEN INC.
Tokyo University of Science, Tohoku University, Nagoya University and Studio Ousia

paper.abstract: We describe tus-nlp’s Lit3R (Retrieve–Relate–Read) system for LitTraceQA, a shared task for literature-grounded question answering that requires systems to retrieve relevant papers, identify supporting evidence, and generate answers. Lit3R combines off-the-shelf retrieval, reranking, and large language model (LLM) components without task-specific training. The retriever iteratively combines BM25-based sparse and dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and LLM-based verification, and complements retrieval based on the question with paper-to-paper expansion. The reader first identifies supporting evidence within individual papers and then synthesizes evidence across papers to produce the final answer and evidence trace. On the official test set, our system ranked 4th on the leaderboard. Our code is available at https://github.com/tus-ist-nlp/littraceqa.

paper.title: Ensar at GroundLM 2026 Shared Tasks: Symbolic Scene Serialisation for View-Level Evidence Identification
paper.abstract: An autonomous vehicle has the privilege of abundant data drawn from many sources, but abundance raises a question of provenance: when we care about one specific event in the scene, which source actually carries the evi dence for it? Identifying that source matters be yond attribution, because a system that weighs every channel at once lets the irrelevant ones di lute the decision, and more input is not the same as more information. GoldenViewVQA poses this question in a controlled form, asking a sys tem to name which of six synchronised vehicle cameras carries the evidence for a question, and to answer that question. We introduce a novel two-stage system built on symbolic scene serialisation. We sweep all six views with a de tector fine-tuned on nuScenes, back-project ev ery detection onto the ground plane, associate detections across cameras into single objects that carry an explicit view-set, and render the scene as text. A language model then names the supporting view and the answer, reading either the serialisation alone (System 1) or the serialisation together with the six raw images (System 2). The pixels help the system locate evidence, not answer questions: System 2 lifts view macro-accuracy to 0.68, against 0.38 for System 1 and 0.14 for an always-CAM_FRONT baseline. Our best run reaches 0.78 joint accu racy, 0.83 view accuracy and 0.65 view macro accuracy on the official test split. Answer accu racy already reaches 0.95 with no image at all: option phrasing alone largely solves the answer head, leaving nearly all the measurable signal in the view head.

paper.title: Efficient Adaptation of Small Language Models for Reliable Mathematical Reasoning
paper.abstract: Efficient training and adaptation are central to deploying language models under resource constraints. We present a controlled comparison of six parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods—LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, LoftQ, and AdaLoRA—across the full cross-product of three base models (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B) and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH), with every configuration trained on MetaMathQA under one identical budget and reported as mean ± standard deviation over three seeds. Qwen2.5-1.5B + PiSSA reaches 71.40 ± 0.27% on GSM8K, exceeding the unadapted 7B base model (68.50 ± 0.42%; Welch’s t(3.4) = 10.06, p = 0.001). Significance testing shows that the method ordering—PiSSA > DoRA > LoRA ≈ AdaLoRA ≈ LoftQ ≈ QLoRA—is identical across all three base models (Kendall’s τ = 1.0), but that only the PiSSA and DoRA gains over LoRA survive multiple-comparison correction: the LoRA/QLoRA/LoftQ/AdaLoRA cluster is statistically indistinguishable at n=3. Four-bit QLoRA cuts peak training VRAM by up to 69.6% (72.8% with PagedAdamW), within one point of the 68.7% predicted by a static-memory model, while PagedAdamW trades 15–20% throughput for memory safety. We add rank and target-module ablations, a GSM8K error taxonomy, and the finding that PiSSA’s spectral initialization at r=16 outperforms LoRA at r=64, and we release the training, evaluation, and profiling code with the exact configuration for every run.

paper.title: Findings of the First GroundLM Shared Tasks: Evaluating Grounded Language Models Across Visual and Scientific Evidence

author.affiliation: Stanford University and University of Waterloo

paper.abstract: The first GroundLM shared tasks evaluate whether language models can identify the evidence behind an answer, rather than merely produce a correct answer in isolation. GoldenViewVQA requires a model to answer a multiple-choice question about six synchronized driving-camera views and identify the supporting view. LitTraceQA requires systems to retrieve scientific papers, locate answer-bearing evidence, and return multiple-choice or structured-table answers. We summarize the task design, submitted systems, official results, and recurrent failure modes. Among teams that submitted system reports, the best official joint accuracy on GoldenViewVQA is 0.8814. Answer accuracy is consistently higher than view accuracy, while macro view accuracy remains lower than micro accuracy, exposing both attribution errors and view imbalance. On the required LitTraceQA test set, the best score among teams that submitted system reports is 0.8002. Paper retrieval approaches saturation for several systems, but evidence F1 and structured-table accuracy remain substantially lower. Across both tasks, the central finding is consistent: producing a correct answer is easier than recovering the exact evidence representation required to justify it. We also report an optional 4,901-question LitTraceQA diagnostic split, whose unverified labels make it useful for stress testing but not for ranking systems on the main task.
